research.summary: I found no published work, as of 2026-09-27, in which an LLM or VLM is itself the metric SLAM estimator: integrating odometry, triangulating landmarks and producing a pose and landmark map with measured trajectory error. In every system I checked, the geometry comes from a classical component. ConceptGraphs takes posed RGB-D frames, SayPlan assumes a pre-built 3D scene graph, VLFM builds its occupancy map from depth, and the 2026 systems use ORB-SLAM3, Cartographer or RTAB-Map. VLG-Loc uses a VLM to find landmarks but computes the pose with Monte Carlo localization. The evidence against pure in-context numeric estimation is consistent. Accuracy collapses as the number of steps grows (Faith and Fate, seqBench, Lost in Aggregation). LLMs do not build cumulative spatial world models (Li 2026). SayPlan's authors report the LLM "fails at simple distance-based reasoning". VLMs are near chance on relative camera pose (best 0.66 vs LoFTR 0.99), and even GPT-5 is still well below humans on spatial benchmarks. The evidence in favour is about the jobs around the estimator. LLMs/VLMs choose exploration frontiers well (VLFM, L3MVN, Aitha 2026 with up to +24% coverage, and Lee 2026, where Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.5 reach over 97% coverage through MCP tools on Isaac Sim with a Nova Carter). They re-rank place-recognition candidates (Lyu 2024) and build or repair topological/semantic maps (MapGPT, LLM-MapRepair, Guide-LLM). They also make discrete decisions on a robot that uses AprilTags as anchors (Syarubany 2026). Tool use and code execution reliably fix LLM arithmetic and spatial computation errors (PAL, SpatialClaw, VADAR). One important caveat: the one text-only LLM exploration benchmark I found gives the model its position for free ("This is not SLAM: the uncertainty is in the map, not in pose"). So "LLM as SLAM" is feasible if the LLM orchestrates numeric tools and does the topological/semantic mapping, data association, loop-closure decisions and exploration. As a pure in-context numeric estimator it can be run and measured, but everything I found predicts it will drift badly. That makes it a sensible, untested baseline arm for the benchmark rather than the main design.

claims.claim: SayPlan (Rana et al., 2023, arXiv:2307.06135, 'SayPlan: Grounding Large Language Models using 3D Scene Graphs for Scalable Robot Task Planning') does not build the map; it assumes a pre-built 3D scene graph, serialized to JSON with metric positions, for the LLM to read.
claims.quote: We assume a pre-constructed 3DSG representation of a large-scale environment generated using existing techniques [15, 13, 11]. The entire 3DSG can be represented as a NetworkX Graph object [42] and text-serialised into a JSON data format that can be parsed directly by a pretrained LLM.

claims.claim: SayPlan's own limitations section says the LLM fails at simple distance and count reasoning over the graph and that the system needs a pre-built, static scene graph. The authors suggest integrating online scene-graph SLAM as future work.
claims.quote: SayPlan is limited by the graph-based reasoning capabilities of the underlying LLM which fails at simple distance-based reasoning, node count-based reasoning and node negation.

claims.claim: SayPlan hands metric path planning to a classical planner (Dijkstra) instead of the LLM.
claims.quote: reduce the planning horizon for the LLM by integrating a classical path planner

claims.claim: ConceptGraphs (Gu et al., 2023, arXiv:2309.16650) builds open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs from already-posed RGB-D frames. The poses come from elsewhere; LLMs/VLMs only supply object captions and tags.
claims.quote: Given a set of posed RGB-D frames, we run a class-agnostic segmentation model to obtain candidate objects, associate them across multiple views using geometric and semantic similarity measures, and instantiate nodes in a 3D scene graph.

claims.claim: HOV-SG (Werby et al., 2024, arXiv:2403.17846) builds a floor/room/object scene graph on top of 3D open-vocabulary segment maps and navigates with a Voronoi graph. The foundation models supply semantics, not pose.
claims.quote: we first obtain state-of-the-art open-vocabulary segment-level maps in 3D and subsequently construct a 3D scene graph hierarchy consisting of floor, room, and object concepts, each enriched with open-vocabulary features

claims.claim: In LM-Nav (Shah et al., 2022, arXiv:2207.04429; just outside the 2023-2026 window), GPT-3 only turns the instruction into a list of textual landmarks. The topological 'mental map' is built from prior observations by a learned visual navigation model, not by the LLM.
claims.quote: given a set of observations in the target environment, the distance predictions from the VNM can be used to construct a topological graph G(V, E) that represents a “mental map” of the environment

claims.claim: NavGPT (Zhou et al., 2023, arXiv:2305.16986) reports that GPT models, given text descriptions of observations and history, can track navigation progress and draw a top-down metric trajectory. Zero-shot R2R performance still falls short of trained models.
claims.quote: as well as drawing accurate top-down metric trajectory given the agent's navigation history. Despite the performance of using NavGPT to zero-shot R2R tasks still falling short of trained models

claims.claim: VLFM (Yokoyama et al., 2023, arXiv:2312.03275) splits the work: frontiers come from a depth-based occupancy map, and the VLM only scores which frontier to explore.
claims.quote: VLFM builds occupancy maps from depth observations to identify frontiers, and leverages RGB observations and a pre-trained vision-language model to generate a language-grounded value map.

claims.claim: L3MVN (Yu et al., 2023, arXiv:2304.05501) uses an LLM to pick the relevant frontier from a semantic map as a long-term goal while exploring unknown environments, with a real-robot test.
claims.quote: use language to find the relevant frontier from the semantic map as a long-term goal and explore the environment efficiently

claims.claim: ESC (Zhou et al., 2023, arXiv:2301.13166) turns LLM/VLM commonsense into soft exploration constraints for zero-shot object navigation, with large gains over CoW.
claims.quote: 288% relative Success Rate improvement than CoW on MP3D

claims.claim: Explore until Confident (Ren et al., 2024, arXiv:2403.15941) states that VLMs have no internal memory for mapping and that their confidence can be miscalibrated. The authors add a depth-based semantic map and conformal calibration.
claims.quote: they do not have an internal memory for mapping the scene to be able to plan how to explore over time, and their confidence can be miscalibrated and can cause the robot to prematurely stop exploration or over-explore

claims.claim: Aitha (2026, arXiv:2605.23165, 'Autonomous Frontier-Based Exploration with VLM Guidance') has a VLM choose frontiers on an RTAB-Map occupancy grid and reports up to 24% more coverage than classical baselines, in simulation only. Gemini 2.5 Pro was chosen over GPT-4o for spatial reasoning.
claims.quote: The VLM analyzes this prompt to select the most promising frontier, replacing simple geometric heuristics with contextual spatial reasoning. This approach, validated in simulation across six indoor environments, improves map coverage by up to 24% over existing methods.

claims.claim: Lee et al. (2026-09-23, arXiv:2609.27340, 'Spatial and Semantic Reasoning for LLM-Driven Robot Navigation via MCP') expose ROS maps to LLMs as MCP tools. Cartographer does the SLAM and Nav2 the navigation, in Isaac Sim with a Nova Carter. Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.5 reach over 97% map coverage.
claims.quote: Cartographer is used for SLAM and Nav2 for navigation. ... The experiment is conducted in the NVIDIA Isaac Sim simulator using a Nova Carter robot. ... The LLM backends used in this study are Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.5, both accessed through the MCP interface.

claims.claim: In the same MCP study, spatial-reasoning navigation succeeded 26/30 times for Claude Sonnet 4.6 and 28/30 for GPT-5.5. Failures came from misreading the map's geometry.
claims.quote: Failures occurred when the LLM misidentified a corridor as a room or incorrectly estimated room sizes, leading to erroneous spatial reasoning and incorrect goal selection.

claims.claim: Sandfuchs et al. (2026, arXiv:2604.09604, 'LLMs for Text-Based Exploration and Navigation under Partial Observability') test nine LLMs as text-only, no-tool controllers in ASCII gridworlds. The agent's pose is given to it (oracle localization), so the benchmark explicitly does not test SLAM.
claims.quote: This is not SLAM: the uncertainty is in the map, not in pose.

claims.claim: In that study, reasoning-tuned models (GPT-5, GPT-OSS-120B) reliably finished navigation while several instruct models failed. The authors recommend calling the LLM only at infrequent decision points because of cost.
claims.quote: From a Green AI perspective, LLM inference is more energy-intensive than classical online planning; hence LLM calls are best gated to infrequent, abstract decision points.

claims.claim: Lost in Aggregation (Jiang et al., 2026, arXiv:2606.22219) finds that end-to-end LLM maze navigation (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Llama-3.3-70B) collapses as mazes grow, even though single-step probes stay far above zero. Handing corridor traversal to a deterministic walker lifts GPT-4o success by up to 92 points.
claims.quote: end-to-end one-shot navigation collapses to near zero by 10×10

claims.claim: Li et al. (2026, arXiv:2604.10690, 'Do LLMs Build Spatial World Models?') find that Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-5-mini, Claude-Haiku-4.5 and DeepSeek do not build cumulative spatial knowledge. Accuracy depends heavily on how the problem is represented.
claims.quote: models fail to leverage this understanding for consistent spatial computations, indicating that they treat each question independently rather than building cumulative spatial knowledge

claims.claim: Martorell (2025, arXiv:2502.16690) finds that explicit Cartesian (x, y) state representations beat topographic and prose representations for LLM grid navigation, and that performance scales with model size.
claims.quote: cartesian representations of space consistently yield higher success rates and path efficiency, with performance scaling markedly with model size

claims.claim: CogEval (Momennejad et al., 2023, arXiv:2309.15129) finds systematic failures in LLM cognitive-map use: hallucinated invalid trajectories and getting stuck in loops.
claims.quote: systematic evaluation reveals striking failure modes in planning tasks, including hallucinations of invalid trajectories and getting trapped in loops

claims.claim: MANGO (Ding et al., 2024, arXiv:2403.19913) finds that GPT-4 performs poorly at mapping and navigation questions over text-game mazes that humans find easy.
claims.quote: even GPT-4, the best-to-date language model, performs poorly at answering them

claims.claim: LLM-MapRepair (Zhang et al., 2025, arXiv:2510.04195) builds navigation graphs incrementally with LLMs and repairs inconsistencies using ideas borrowed from SLAM. With GPT-4.1, edge recall rises sharply, but the graphs over-generate nodes and edges (about 4x ground truth).
claims.quote: 94.3% node recall (+8.6 pp over direct LLM mapping) and 88.2% edge recall (+55.8 pp)

claims.claim: Lost in Space (Deng et al., 2026, arXiv:2601.22228) shows VLMs are poor at relative camera pose from image pairs: best VLM 0.66 vs LoFTR 0.99 and humans 0.91. They are also inconsistent when source and target images are swapped.
claims.quote: unstable under source-target reversal (best 59.7% consistency)

claims.claim: STI-Bench (Li et al., 2025, arXiv:2503.23765) finds MLLMs struggle with quantitative displacement, speed and trajectory estimation; top models score at most about 50% overall.
claims.quote: struggle to accurately calculate and describe motion characteristics like displacement, speed, and trajectories

claims.claim: VSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2024, arXiv:2412.14171, 'Thinking in Space') finds spatial reasoning is the main bottleneck for MLLMs. Chain-of-thought does not help, but having the model generate an explicit cognitive map does improve distance reasoning.
claims.quote: spatial reasoning capabilities remain the primary bottleneck

claims.claim: EASI (Cai et al., 2025, arXiv:2508.13142) finds GPT-5 is the strongest model on spatial intelligence but still well below humans.
claims.quote: GPT-5 demonstrates unprecedented strength in SI, yet still falls short of human performance significantly

claims.claim: ESI-Bench (Hong et al., 2026, arXiv:2605.18746) finds MLLM agents choose poor exploratory actions ('action blindness') and, unlike humans, commit to answers with high confidence regardless of evidence quality.
claims.quote: commit prematurely with high confidence regardless of evidence quality

claims.claim: VLN-MME (Zhao et al., 2025, arXiv:2512.24851) finds MLLM navigation agents have low 3D spatial-reasoning fidelity, and adding chain-of-thought and self-reflection lowered performance.
claims.quote: MLLMs exhibit poor context awareness in embodied navigation tasks; although they can follow instructions and structure their output, their 3D spatial reasoning fidelity is low

claims.claim: SpatialVLM (Chen et al., 2024, arXiv:2401.12168) states that VLMs lack quantitative 3D reasoning such as distances.
claims.quote: still lack capabilities in 3D spatial reasoning, such as recognizing quantitative relationships of physical objects like distances or size differences

claims.claim: Faith and Fate (Dziri et al., 2023, arXiv:2305.18654) shows transformer LLM accuracy decays quickly as the number of composed steps grows, for example in multi-digit multiplication. This is the same mechanism that would make running odometry sums drift.
claims.quote: autoregressive generations' performance can rapidly decay with increased task complexity

claims.claim: seqBench (Ramezanali et al., 2025, arXiv:2509.16866) finds LLM accuracy collapses exponentially once the number of sequential steps passes a model-specific limit.
claims.quote: accuracy collapses exponentially beyond a model-specific logical depth

claims.claim: Lost in the Middle (Liu et al., 2023, arXiv:2307.03172) shows LLMs use information in the middle of long contexts poorly. That matters when a growing observation log is kept in the prompt.
claims.quote: performance can degrade significantly when changing the position of relevant information, indicating that current language models do not robustly make use of information in long input contexts

claims.claim: PAL (Gao et al., 2022, arXiv:2211.10435) shows LLMs decompose problems well but make arithmetic mistakes, and that handing the computation to a Python interpreter improves accuracy.
claims.quote: LLMs often make logical and arithmetic mistakes in the solution part, even when the problem is decomposed correctly

claims.claim: SpatialClaw (Cho et al., 2026, arXiv:2606.13673) gives a VLM agent a stateful Python kernel with geometry primitives, using code as its action interface. It beats a prior spatial agent across 20 benchmarks and six backbones.
claims.quote: SpatialClaw achieves 59.9% average accuracy, outperforming the recent spatial agent by +11.2 points, with consistent gains across six VLM backbones from two model families

claims.claim: VADAR (Marsili et al., 2025, arXiv:2502.06787) has LLM agents synthesize a Python API for 3D spatial reasoning, and it outperforms prior zero-shot models.
claims.quote: their performance declines when tasked with 3D spatial reasoning. To tackle the complexity of such reasoning problems, we introduce an agentic program synthesis approach

claims.claim: Tell Me Where You Are (Lyu et al., 2024, arXiv:2406.17520) uses a vision foundation model to retrieve place-recognition candidates and an MLLM to compare them pair by pair, with no VPR-specific training. This is the LLM-in-the-loop form of place recognition and loop closure.
claims.quote: Our key design is to use vision-based retrieval to propose several candidates and then leverage language-based reasoning to carefully inspect each candidate for a final decision.

claims.claim: ROVER (Yu et al., 2025, arXiv:2508.13488) criticizes an ICRA 2024 LLM-assisted loop-closure method (cited as H. Li et al.): it relies on unverifiable LLM reasoning, is not real-time, and struggles with repeated semantic entities.
claims.quote: Moreover, it heavily relies on the reasoning ability of an LLM, which is not certifiable and struggles to achieve real-time performance.

claims.claim: VLG-Loc (Aoki et al., 2025, arXiv:2512.12793) has a VLM search for map landmarks in images, but the pose is computed by Monte Carlo localization, not by the VLM.
claims.quote: The method then identifies robot poses within a Monte Carlo localization framework, where the found landmarks are used to evaluate the likelihood of each pose hypothesis.

claims.claim: Mobility VLA (Chiang et al., 2024, arXiv:2407.07775) uses Gemini 1.5 Pro over a tour video plus a topological graph built offline with COLMAP. It reaches 86%/90% success, but the VLM takes 10-30 s per query, so it is called only for goal selection.
claims.quote: the high-level VLM spends 10-30s to find a goal index

claims.claim: MapGPT (Chen et al., 2024, arXiv:2401.07314) puts an online topological map, written as text, into GPT-4 prompts for zero-shot VLN, because earlier agents lacked a global view.
claims.quote: without constructing an effective 'global-view' for the agent to understand the overall environment

claims.claim: Syarubany et al. (2026, arXiv:2601.00555) is the closest prior system to this project. An LLM explores via discrete choices in Gazebo and a real corridor, uses AprilTags as anchors, and stores a JSON semantic map. ORB-SLAM3 supplies the pose, and only qualitative results are reported.
claims.quote: an LLM produces a constrained discrete action at each junction (direction and whether to enter a store)

claims.claim: In Syarubany et al., AprilTags anchor the semantic map, and continuous pose comes from SLAM, not from the LLM.
claims.quote: SLAM to provide a continuous global pose estimate that downstream modules can use for logging motion primitives

claims.claim: RoboAtlas (Schperberg et al., 2026, arXiv:2606.26046) is an 'Active SLAM' system where a contextual bandit switches between geometric frontier exploration and VLM reasoning. The geometric mapping stays classical.
claims.quote: integrates frontier exploration, global semantic-map reasoning, and egocentric VLM-based reasoning through a contextual multi-armed bandit

claims.claim: In published 'LLM + SLAM' systems, the LLM supplies priors or semantics, not pose. Jiao et al. (2025, arXiv:2509.21602) add LLM object-size and orientation priors as factors; SEO-SLAM (Hong et al., 2024, arXiv:2411.06752) uses MLLMs for semantics and solves data association as a linear assignment; LP-SLAM (Zhang et al., 2023, arXiv:2303.10089) uses the LLM to decide which scene text is a landmark.
claims.quote: leveraging large language models (LLMs) to provide commonsense knowledge of object geometric attributes, specifically size and orientation, as prior factors in a graph-based SLAM framework

claims.claim: SEO-SLAM's data association combines semantic and Mahalanobis costs in a linear assignment problem instead of letting the MLLM decide matches directly.
claims.quote: a multi-data association strategy using a cost matrix that combines semantic and Mahalanobis distances, formulating the problem as a Linear Assignment Problem (LAP) to alleviate perceptual aliasing

claims.claim: Barkley et al. (2025, arXiv:2505.01931) test GPT-4 as a path planner on a low-cost robot localized by an overhead camera. A* is faster and more accurate for geometric routes; GPT-4 adds value only on semantic constraints.
claims.quote: while A* is faster and more accurate for basic route generation and obstacle avoidance, the GPT-4-integrated system achieves high success rates (96-100%) on semantic tasks that are infeasible for pure geometric planners

claims.claim: A 2026 Sensors paper ('A Large Language Model-Guided IMU-PDR Method for Detection and Error Correction', Sensors 26(18):5897) prompts an LLM to guide step detection, heading correction and trajectory reconstruction for pedestrian dead reckoning. It claims reduced heading drift; I saw only the search snippet (the page returned 403).
claims.quote: incorporates domain-specific prior knowledge into prompts to guide the LLM in step-count detection, step-length estimation, heading correction, and subsequent trajectory reconstruction

claims.claim: ReMEmbR (Anwar et al., 2024, arXiv:2409.13682) stores robot memory with positions and time in a retrieval database queried by an LLM, and outperforms plain LLM/VLM long-context baselines.
claims.quote: Our experiments demonstrate that ReMEmbR outperforms LLM and VLM baselines, allowing ReMEmbR to achieve effective long-horizon reasoning with low latency.

claims.claim: Guide-LLM (Song et al., 2024, arXiv:2410.20666) gives an LLM a text-based topological map (straight paths and right-angle turns) for global planning. This shows the kind of simplified map representation an LLM can work with directly.
claims.quote: a novel text-based topological map that enables the LLM to plan global paths using a simplified environmental representation, focusing on straight paths and right-angle turns

claims.claim: ABot-Explorer (Chen et al., 2026, arXiv:2604.19034) uses VLMs to pick out navigational affordances such as doorways and builds a hierarchical scene-graph memory online from RGB alone.
claims.quote: unifies memory construction and exploration into an online, RGB-only process

claims.claim: Monocular-only navigation models exist for the VLA/navigation-foundation-model arm. Robostral Navigate (2026, arXiv:2607.20785) is an 8B VLM that predicts image-space waypoints from monocular RGB and reports 77.4% on R2R-CE. VL-Explore (Zhang et al., 2025, arXiv:2502.08791) explores with monocular vision and no prior map.
claims.quote: The model consumes only a stream of monocular RGB images - the most ubiquitous sensor across robotic platforms and predicts waypoints by pointing to the next target location in the current camera view.

claims.claim: NoMaD (Sridhar et al., 2023, arXiv:2310.07896) is a navigation foundation policy that handles both goal-directed navigation and task-agnostic exploration in unfamiliar environments. It outputs actions, not an explicit pose or map estimate.
claims.quote: Robotic learning for navigation in unfamiliar environments needs to provide policies for both task-oriented navigation (i.e., reaching a goal that the robot has located), and task-agnostic exploration (i.e., searching for a goal in a novel setting).

implications: (Inference) Feasibility verdict: the project is feasible if 'LLM as SLAM' means the LLM runs the SLAM process: deciding what counts as a landmark, data association, accepting loop closures, choosing where to explore, keeping a topological/semantic beacon map, and detecting anomalies such as wheel slip or a kidnapped robot. The numbers (odometry integration, tag range/bearing from AprilTag PnP, pose-graph optimization) come from deterministic tools it calls. This is what every 2024-2026 working system does (Lee 2026 MCP, Aitha 2026, VLG-Loc, Syarubany 2026).

(Inference) Pure in-context numeric SLAM, where the LLM reads odometry deltas and tag observations as text and writes out poses and landmark coordinates, can be run, but it should be a baseline or ablation arm, not the main design. The literature predicts drift and inconsistency that grow with the number of steps (Faith and Fate, seqBench, Lost in Aggregation, Li 2026). I found no paper that measures it, so reporting trajectory error (ATE) for a pure-LLM estimator against a classical EKF or iSAM2 on the same data would be a genuinely new result, even if negative.

(Inference) Suggested benchmark design, a ladder of how much the LLM is responsible for: L0 is a classical estimator (EKF-SLAM or GTSAM iSAM2 on odometry plus AprilTag range/bearing). L1 has the LLM do the numeric estimation in context, with JSON Cartesian state (Martorell 2025) and a compact rolling state summary instead of the full history (Lost in the Middle). L2 lets the LLM call numeric tools such as integrate_odometry, triangulate, optimize_pose_graph and query_map (PAL, SpatialClaw). L3 makes the LLM responsible only for semantic/topological mapping, loop-closure decisions and frontier choice on top of L0. Scoring on the same recorded data lets every model be compared fairly.

(Inference) Metrics: ATE/RPE after alignment; beacon-map error (landmark RMSE after a Procrustes/Umeyama fit); loop-closure precision and recall; data-association error rate; exploration coverage against steps and distance; number of invalid or hallucinated map entries (LLM-MapRepair over-generates); and consistency, measured as NEES if the model reports covariance. Also track tokens, dollars and wall-clock latency per decision. ESI-Bench's overconfidence finding suggests measuring calibration explicitly.

(Inference) Offline replay is the key to fair model comparison. Record the sim and real runs (rosbags of odometry, IMU and tag detections), turn them into identical text or tool streams, and replay the same streams to GPT 6 Astra/Sol, Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and the local Qwen/Gemma models. Closed-loop runs, where the model's own mistakes change what the robot sees next, can then be a smaller second tier.

(Inference) Unique AprilTag 36h11 IDs make data association and loop closure almost trivial for classical code, which leaves the LLM little real SLAM work. To give it a real job, the benchmark could include conditions with aliased beacons (duplicate IDs, or IDs hidden so the model only knows 'a tag'), or require tag-free place recognition from ESP32-CAM images. The latter is the LLM4VPR pattern, which ROVER warns is slow and unverifiable in repetitive scenes.

(Inference) Do not ask the VLM to read pose from raw camera frames. The best VLM scores 0.66 on relative pose vs 0.99 for LoFTR (Lost in Space), and VLMs lack quantitative distance skills (SpatialVLM, STI-Bench). Give the LLM classical AprilTag detector output (ID, range, bearing, reprojection error) as structured text, and use images only for semantic context and revisit confirmation.

(Inference) Hardware fit: VLFM-style exploration relies on depth-derived occupancy maps, and this robot has no range sensor. Frontiers should therefore be defined over the beacon and topological graph ('unexplored bearing from tag 7') or come from sparse monocular cues. RGB-only systems such as ABot-Explorer, VL-Explore and Robostral show that monocular exploration is possible, but not with metric occupancy.

(Inference) Latency and control: VLM calls took 10-30 s in Mobility VLA, and Sandfuchs et al. recommend calling the LLM only at infrequent decision points. A stop-observe-think-move protocol fits the constraint that the LLM stays out of the motor loop: the robot stops, the LLM reasons, then it issues one bounded move for the Pico 2 W to execute. A frontier API model's round-trip time will set how fast the robot can explore.

(Inference) Expect a gap between model tiers. Reasoning-tuned models finished navigation reliably where instruct models failed (Sandfuchs 2026), and GPT-5.5 beat Claude Sonnet 4.6 by 2/30 trials in Lee 2026. For the smaller local models (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B), the tool-augmented arm will probably matter more than for frontier models. This is untested.

(Inference) VLA and navigation foundation models (Robostral Navigate, NoMaD) output actions or waypoints and keep no explicit pose or beacon map, so trajectory and map-error metrics cannot score them directly. Put them only in the exploration and coverage tasks, or pair them with the L0 estimator to read out their trajectory.

(Inference) Framing risk: presenting the project as 'the LLM replaces the SLAM estimator' invites the result 'it does worse than EKF'. A more defensible research question is 'which parts of landmark SLAM can an LLM own, and how much does accuracy and cost change at each level of the ladder?' Isaac Sim with Nova Carter (the setting of Lee 2026) and Gazebo Harmonic both match the student's existing setup.
unknowns: I found no paper, 2023-2026, that evaluates an LLM or VLM doing in-context landmark SLAM or EKF-style estimation (odometry plus range/bearing to beacons) and reports trajectory error (ATE/RPE) or map error. So there is no quantitative prior for how badly the pure in-context arm will drift.

I found no source for an LLM agent calling a pose-graph or factor-graph solver (GTSAM, g2o, iSAM2) as a tool. The closest is Lee 2026, where Cartographer runs underneath and the LLM only reads map images through MCP.
I found no evidence on whether VLMs can decode AprilTag/ArUco IDs directly from images, including the low-quality JPEG from an ESP32-CAM/OV3660.

I found no benchmark results for the specific models the student named (GPT 6 Astra, GPT 6 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1). The newest models in the sources are GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5.
I found no data comparing the locally cached open models (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Qwen3.8-27B-FP8, Gemma-4-26B-A4B) with frontier models on spatial or state-tracking tasks, nor their latency on a DGX Spark.

Authorship of the ICRA 2024 paper 'Resolving loop closure confusion in repetitive environments for visual SLAM through AI foundation models assistance' is unconfirmed. ROVER cites H. Li, S. Yu, S. Zhang, G. Tan, but one search snippet named different authors, and I did not fetch the paper itself.
The details of the LLM-guided IMU-PDR paper (Sensors 2026) are unverified: the MDPI page returned 403, so I saw only the search-result snippet and no error numbers.
The STI-Bench numbers come from the project page, not the arXiv paper, and the exact VSI-Bench per-task and human numbers were not verified verbatim.
HOV-SG's input assumption (posed RGB-D) was not confirmed from the abstract. Syarubany 2026 does not name its LLM and reports no quantitative success rates.
It is untested how LLMs handle beacon aliasing (duplicate or hidden tag IDs), or loop closure when IDs are unique, which could make the LLM's role trivial.

I found no study of LLM exploration or localization on a robot with only a monocular camera plus wheel odometry and no range sensor. All the LLM frontier-exploration systems I found use depth or lidar occupancy maps.

verdicts.claim: SayPlan (arXiv:2307.06135) assumes a pre-built 3D scene graph, text-serialised to JSON with metric positions; it does not build the map.
verdicts.note: I downloaded the PDF, and the quote is verbatim on the page: 'We assume a pre-constructed 3DSG representation ... text-serialised into a JSON data format'. The example node has 'position: [2.34, 0.45, 2.23]'.

verdicts.claim: SayPlan's limitations say the LLM fails at distance, count and negation reasoning and that the system needs a pre-built static graph; the authors suggest online scene-graph SLAM as future work.
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'fails at simple distance-based reasoning, node count-based reasoning and node negation' and 'constrained by the need for a pre-built 3D scene graph and assumes that objects remain static post-map generation ... Future work could explore how online scene graph SLAM systems [15] could be integrated'. Small precision point: 'static' refers to the objects, not the graph.

verdicts.claim: SayPlan hands metric path planning to a classical planner (Dijkstra).
verdicts.note: The abstract says 'integrating a classical path planner'. The PDF says 'delegating pose-level path planning to an optimal path planner, such as Dijkstra'.

verdicts.claim: ConceptGraphs (arXiv:2309.16650) builds scene graphs from already-posed RGB-D frames; LLMs/VLMs only supply captions and tags.
verdicts.note: The quote about posed RGB-D frames is verbatim. But the LLM also 'infer[s] spatial relationships between objects to construct graph edges', so it does more than captions and tags. On real robots the poses come from Open3D SLAM (LiDAR) or RTAB-Map. This supports the researcher's main point that the geometry is classical.

verdicts.claim: HOV-SG (arXiv:2403.17846) builds a floor/room/object graph on open-vocabulary segment maps and navigates with a Voronoi graph; the foundation models supply semantics, not pose.
verdicts.note: The abstract confirms 'cross-floor Voronoi graph' and real-world multi-storey robot navigation. The abstract does not state the posed RGB-D input, as the researcher already noted, so 'not pose' is inference.

verdicts.claim: LM-Nav (arXiv:2207.04429): GPT-3 only parses landmarks; the topological 'mental map' is built by the VNM (ViNG).
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the PDF text: 'the distance predictions from the VNM can be used to construct a topological graph G(V, E) that represents a "mental map"'. Also 'the LLM, which parses user instructions into a list of landmarks'.

verdicts.claim: NavGPT (arXiv:2305.16986) can draw an accurate top-down metric trajectory from navigation history; its zero-shot R2R results fall short of trained models.
verdicts.note: Both quotes are verbatim in the abstract. Caveat: this is a qualitative claim on R2R, a discrete navigation graph with textual observation descriptions. It is not an ATE measurement. It is also the one piece of evidence that partly favours in-context metric tracking, and the researcher did not weigh it in the summary.

verdicts.claim: VLFM (arXiv:2312.03275): frontiers come from a depth-based occupancy map, and the VLM only scores them.
verdicts.note: I did not re-fetch this page. The quote matches the well-known abstract wording, but I did not independently confirm it in this pass.

verdicts.claim: L3MVN (arXiv:2304.05501) uses an LLM to pick frontiers from a semantic map, with a real-robot test.
verdicts.note: The abstract says: 'we provide a real robot experiment to verify the applicability of our framework in real-world scenarios.'

verdicts.claim: ESC (arXiv:2301.13166) turns commonsense into soft exploration constraints, with a 288% relative SR gain over CoW on MP3D.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim. The result is from simulation only (MP3D, HM3D, RoboTHOR).

verdicts.claim: Explore until Confident (arXiv:2403.15941): VLMs lack internal mapping memory and have miscalibrated confidence; the authors add a depth-based semantic map and conformal calibration.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim, the method uses depth, and there are real-robot experiments.

verdicts.claim: Aitha 2026 (arXiv:2605.23165): a VLM picks frontiers on an RTAB-Map grid, with up to +24% coverage, simulation only; Gemini 2.5 Pro was chosen over GPT-4o.
verdicts.note: Confirmed: RTAB-Map on ROS Noetic, simulation-only results (sim-to-real is deferred to a thesis), and Gemini 2.5 Pro chosen for 'superior spatial and strategic reasoning'. Missing context that matters for this robot: the occupancy map comes from an RGB-D camera via depthimage_to_laserscan, i.e. a depth sensor.

verdicts.claim: Lee et al. 2026 (arXiv:2609.27340): Cartographer for SLAM and Nav2 for navigation, in Isaac Sim with a Nova Carter; Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.5 reach over 97% coverage.
verdicts.note: Authors are Jungsoo Lee, Jaegyun Park and Wansoo Kim, dated 2026-09-23. Coverage is 97.83% for Sonnet 4.6 and 99.78% for GPT-5.5. Simulation only, with no real robot. The LLM receives the occupancy grid as an annotated image through MCP tools (subscribe_map_as_image, draw_map_axis, draw_robot_pose). The paper does not describe any algorithmic frontier computation, and it reports no latency.

verdicts.claim: Lee 2026 spatial-reasoning navigation: 26/30 (Sonnet 4.6) vs 28/30 (GPT-5.5); failures came from misreading map geometry.
verdicts.note: Confirmed: 86.67% vs 93.33%, and failures 'misidentified a corridor as a room or incorrectly estimated room sizes'. Semantic navigation (Task 3) was 30/30 for both models.

verdicts.claim: Sandfuchs et al. 2026 (arXiv:2604.09604): nine LLMs as text-only, no-tool controllers in gridworlds, with oracle pose: 'This is not SLAM'.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim, tools are explicitly prohibited, and localization is oracle. The models include open-weight Gemma-3-27B, Qwen3-235B, QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-OSS-120B. The fetched page shows the date as March 10, 2026, even though the ID prefix is 2604.

verdicts.claim: In Sandfuchs, reasoning models (GPT-5, GPT-OSS-120B) reliably completed navigation while instruct models failed; the authors recommend gating LLM calls to infrequent decision points.
verdicts.note: GPT-5, GPT-OSS-120B and GPT-5-mini all reached 100% success. The full quote continues: '...with high-rate control and path optimisation left to classical algorithms'.

verdicts.claim: Lost in Aggregation (Jiang et al. 2026, arXiv:2606.22219): end-to-end maze navigation collapses by 10x10; a deterministic corridor walker lifts GPT-4o by up to 92 points.
verdicts.note: Confirmed, with an omitted caveat: the delegation gain is at mid-sized mazes and 'diminished at larger scales (30×30)'. Isolated single-step probes stay at 30-75% at 10x10.

verdicts.claim: Li et al. 2026 (arXiv:2604.10690): Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-5-mini, Claude-Haiku-4.5 and DeepSeek do not build cumulative spatial knowledge; accuracy depends on representation.
verdicts.note: Confirmed. The representation effect is large: Gemini drops from 80-86% with tokenized input to 16-34% with visual grids. That is relevant to deciding whether to give maps as images or as text.

verdicts.claim: Martorell 2025 (arXiv:2502.16690): Cartesian representations beat topographic and prose representations; performance scales with model size.
verdicts.note: The Cartesian and model-size quote is verbatim. I did not verify the names of the specific competing formats ('topographic', 'prose').

verdicts.claim: CogEval (arXiv:2309.15129): LLMs hallucinate invalid trajectories and get trapped in loops.
verdicts.note: Verbatim. This is 2023-era evidence (GPT-4, Claude-1), so it may be outdated for 2026 reasoning models.

verdicts.claim: MANGO (arXiv:2403.19913): GPT-4 performs poorly at mapping and navigation questions over text mazes.
verdicts.note: Verbatim. This is also 2024-era, GPT-4 evidence.

verdicts.claim: LLM-MapRepair (arXiv:2510.04195): builds graphs incrementally and repairs them with SLAM-borrowed ideas; with GPT-4.1, edge recall rises sharply but graphs over-generate about 4x.
verdicts.note: The numbers and the roughly 4x over-generation are verbatim in the abstract. The paper cites SLAM and loop closure as foundations. The abstract title is 'Constructing coherent spatial memory in LLM agents through graph rectification'. It is evaluated only on text worlds (TextWorld, MANGO IF maps, a novel), not on robots or sensor data.

verdicts.claim: Lost in Space (Deng et al. 2026, arXiv:2601.22228): best VLM 0.66 vs LoFTR 0.99 vs humans 0.91; best consistency under swap 59.7%.
verdicts.note: All numbers are in the abstract, which was revised 2026-04-29.

verdicts.claim: STI-Bench (arXiv:2503.23765): MLLMs struggle with displacement, speed and trajectory; top models score at most about 50%.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim. The top model on the project page is Gemini-2.5-Pro at 41.4%, and 50% is a threshold the page cites, not the ceiling. 'At most ~50%' is loose; 'best is about 41%' is accurate.

verdicts.claim: VSI-Bench (arXiv:2412.14171): spatial reasoning is the bottleneck; CoT does not help; generating cognitive maps helps distance.
verdicts.note: All three points are verbatim in the abstract.

verdicts.claim: EASI (arXiv:2508.13142): GPT-5 is the strongest but still well below humans.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim, from the version dated Dec 30, 2025. It predates GPT-5.5 and GPT-6, so it may be outdated for the models the student named.

verdicts.claim: ESI-Bench (arXiv:2605.18746): action blindness, and models commit prematurely with high confidence.
verdicts.note: Both phrases are in the abstract.

verdicts.claim: VLN-MME (arXiv:2512.24851): low 3D spatial fidelity; CoT and self-reflection reduced performance.
verdicts.note: The abstract says CoT and self-reflection 'leads to an unexpected performance decrease'.

verdicts.claim: SpatialVLM (arXiv:2401.12168): VLMs lack quantitative 3D reasoning such as distances.
verdicts.note: Verbatim. This is January 2024 evidence about the VLMs of that time.

verdicts.claim: Faith and Fate (arXiv:2305.18654): accuracy decays quickly with the number of composed steps; the same mechanism would make odometry sums drift.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim, from tasks such as multiplication, logic grids and dynamic programming. Applying it to odometry integration is the researcher's inference, not something the paper shows. The evidence is from 2023 models, before reasoning models; Sandfuchs 2026 shows reasoning models doing much better on sequential grid navigation.

verdicts.claim: seqBench (arXiv:2509.16866): accuracy collapses exponentially beyond a model-specific logical depth.
verdicts.note: Verbatim, first author Ramezanali, Sept 2025.

verdicts.claim: Lost in the Middle (arXiv:2307.03172): mid-context information is used poorly.
verdicts.note: Verbatim. It is 2023 evidence and says nothing about 2026 frontier long-context models, but it still supports the idea of a rolling state summary.

verdicts.claim: PAL (arXiv:2211.10435): LLMs make arithmetic mistakes; offloading to Python improves accuracy.
verdicts.note: Verbatim.

verdicts.claim: SpatialClaw (arXiv:2606.13673): code-as-action with a stateful Python kernel; 59.9% average, +11.2 points, 20 benchmarks, six backbones.
verdicts.note: Confirmed. These are image and video spatial QA benchmarks, not robot state estimation.

verdicts.claim: VADAR (arXiv:2502.06787): LLM agents synthesize a Python API for 3D spatial reasoning and outperform prior zero-shot models.
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'outperforms prior zero-shot models for visual reasoning in 3D'. This is static-image 3D QA.

verdicts.claim: Tell Me Where You Are (Lyu 2024, arXiv:2406.17520): VFM retrieval plus MLLM pairwise inspection, with no VPR-specific training.
verdicts.note: The abstract confirms the design and the absence of VPR-specific supervised training. Calling it 'the LLM-in-the-loop form of loop closure' is the researcher's framing; the paper is about place recognition.

verdicts.claim: ROVER (arXiv:2508.13488) criticizes the ICRA 2024 LLM-assisted loop-closure method as uncertifiable, not real-time, and weak with repeated semantic entities.
verdicts.note: Both quotes are verbatim. ROVER's reference [2] lists H. Li, S. Yu, S. Zhang, G. Tan, ICRA 2024, pp. 6657-6663. It also notes trouble with 'scenes without textual information'.

verdicts.claim: VLG-Loc (arXiv:2512.12793): the VLM finds landmarks, and Monte Carlo localization computes the pose.
verdicts.note: Confirmed. The researcher left out that VLG-Loc needs a known 'labeled footprint map', so it is global localization in a known map, not SLAM. It has real-world retail experiments.

verdicts.claim: Mobility VLA (arXiv:2407.07775): Gemini 1.5 Pro, a COLMAP-built topological graph, 86%/90% success, 10-30 s per VLM query.
verdicts.note: Confirmed. The latency comes from a roughly 1M-token tour-video context, which is 99.9% of the input tokens, so it does not generalise to short structured-text calls.

verdicts.claim: MapGPT (arXiv:2401.07314) puts an online topological map, as text, into GPT-4 prompts because earlier agents lacked a global view.
verdicts.note: The map is text in the prompt, but the nodes and edges come from the simulator: 'the simulator will provide several neighboring nodes that are currently navigable'. So the LLM does not build the topology or do the geometry. I did not see the exact 'global-view' phrase on the page summary.

verdicts.claim: Syarubany et al. 2026 (arXiv:2601.00555): the LLM makes discrete junction choices in Gazebo and a real corridor, with AprilTag anchors, a JSON semantic map and ORB-SLAM3 pose; results are qualitative.
verdicts.note: Confirmed. The LLM is not named. The authors are from KAIST. There are no numeric metrics.

verdicts.claim: In Syarubany, AprilTags anchor the map, and continuous pose comes from SLAM.
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'we rely on SLAM to provide a continuous global pose estimate'. The tags are 'reliable junction/entrance references that help stabilize the semantic map'.

verdicts.claim: RoboAtlas (arXiv:2606.26046): Active SLAM with a contextual bandit over frontier, semantic-map and VLM arms; the geometric mapping stays classical.
verdicts.note: Confirmed. Mapping is done by OpenRoboVox (3D semantic mapping). It was also tested on a real Unitree Go2 over areas larger than 1800 m2, which the researcher left out.

verdicts.claim: LLM+SLAM systems use the LLM for priors or semantics, not pose (Jiao 2025, SEO-SLAM, LP-SLAM).
verdicts.note: Jiao, Qiu and Christensen confirm LLM priors on object size and orientation in graph SLAM, with a 36.8% mapping-accuracy gain. LP-SLAM's landmark-text role appears in a search snippet. I did not fetch the exact abstract wording of the Jiao quote verbatim.

verdicts.claim: SEO-SLAM data association uses a LAP with semantic and Mahalanobis costs.
verdicts.note: The abstract confirms the LAP combining semantic similarity and Mahalanobis distance. First author is Jungseok Hong.

verdicts.claim: Barkley 2025 (arXiv:2505.01931): overhead-camera localization; A* is better for geometry, GPT-4 for semantic tasks.
verdicts.note: Verbatim. The robot is a Petoi Bittle with a Pi Zero 2W, localized by an overhead camera.

verdicts.claim: The Sensors 2026 LLM-guided IMU-PDR paper claims reduced heading drift.
verdicts.note: The MDPI page returned 403 to me as well. I could not confirm the content or any numbers.

verdicts.claim: ReMEmbR (arXiv:2409.13682) outperforms LLM/VLM long-context baselines.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim, and it was deployed on a real robot. The positions it stores come from the robot's own localization, not from the LLM.

verdicts.claim: Guide-LLM (arXiv:2410.20666) gives an LLM a text-based topological map for global planning.
verdicts.note: Confirmed. The map is provided to the LLM, which does not build it, and the experiments are simulated only. So the summary's 'build or repair ... maps (... Guide-LLM)' overstates what it shows.

verdicts.claim: ABot-Explorer (arXiv:2604.19034) uses VLM navigational affordances and builds an online RGB-only scene-graph memory.
verdicts.note: The abstract title is 'Explore Like Humans: Autonomous Exploration with Online SG-Memo Construction for Embodied Agents'. The phrase 'online, RGB-only process' is confirmed. I found no evidence of real-robot deployment; the evaluation is on an extended InteriorGS dataset in simulation.

verdicts.claim: Robostral Navigate (arXiv:2607.20785): an 8B monocular VLM, 77.4% on R2R-CE. VL-Explore (arXiv:2502.08791): monocular exploration without a prior map.
verdicts.note: Both are confirmed. VL-Explore uses CLIP, not an LLM or VLA, although it did run on a real UGV. Robostral's R2R-CE number is a simulation benchmark.

verdicts.claim: NoMaD (arXiv:2310.07896) handles goal-directed navigation and exploration and outputs actions, not pose or map.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim, and it has real-robot experiments. It is a diffusion policy, not a language model.

implication_challenges: Implication 1 overstates the precedent. It says 'this is what every working 2024-2026 system does (Lee, Aitha, VLG-Loc, Syarubany)', but none of those systems has the LLM run the SLAM process by calling numeric tools. In each one a classical SLAM or MCL stack runs on its own underneath (Cartographer, RTAB-Map, ORB-SLAM3, MCL), and the LLM only chooses goals or frontiers. In Lee 2026 the LLM reads a rendered map image. No source shows an LLM owning data association or accepting loop closures through tool calls. The only LLM loop-closure evidence (Lyu 2024, and the ICRA 2024 work criticised by ROVER) is place-recognition re-ranking, and ROVER calls it 'not certifiable' and not real-time. 'LLM orchestrates the estimator' is therefore a new design, not an established pattern.

The summary says LLMs 'build or repair topological/semantic maps (MapGPT, LLM-MapRepair, Guide-LLM)'. That is overstated. MapGPT's nodes and edges come from the simulator's navigable-viewpoint graph. Guide-LLM is given a pre-built map and was tested only in simulation. LLM-MapRepair works only on text-adventure and novel text, not sensor data.

Implication 2 treats Faith and Fate, CogEval, MANGO, SpatialVLM and Lost in the Middle as predicting failure for 2026 models, but all of them are 2023-2024 evidence from GPT-3.5/4-era models. Sandfuchs 2026 found reasoning models (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, GPT-OSS-120B) at 100% on sequential grid navigation where instruct models failed. NavGPT also reports 'accurate top-down metric trajectory' drawing from history. The prior for pure in-context estimation by GPT-6-class or Fable 5.1-class reasoning models is genuinely uncertain, not 'will drift badly'. 'Unmeasured' is right; 'predicted to drift badly' is stronger than the evidence.

Implication 9 infers a tier gap from Lee 2026's 26/30 vs 28/30. A two-trial difference over n=30 is not statistically meaningful, and both models tied at 30/30 on semantic navigation. Sandfuchs supports a reasoning-vs-instruct gap; Lee does not support a GPT-5.5 > Sonnet 4.6 ordering.

The latency implication generalises Mobility VLA's 10-30 s, but that figure comes from roughly 1M-token tour-video contexts (99.9% of the input tokens). It does not transfer to short structured-text tool calls. Lee 2026 reports no latency at all. The stop-think-move protocol is sound, but the cited number is not evidence of per-decision cost for this design.

The claim that Isaac Sim with Nova Carter matches the student's setup is misleading for this project. Lee 2026 used Cartographer on the Nova Carter's sensors, and the student's car has no lidar or depth sensor. A Nova Carter sim would give the LLM arms geometric information the real robot cannot produce. The simulated robot must be the student's own differential-drive car with a monocular camera, encoders and IMU, or the sim-to-real comparison is invalid.

Implication 8 lists ABot-Explorer, VL-Explore and Robostral as showing monocular exploration. None of them is LLM-driven landmark SLAM. VL-Explore uses CLIP, ABot-Explorer has no evidence of a real robot, and Robostral is instruction-following VLN (R2R-CE, a simulation benchmark). They show RGB-only navigation policies, not monocular metric mapping.

Implication 7 (give the LLM tag detector output as text, not images) is well supported. Li 2026 adds a further supporting data point: Gemini accuracy fell from 80-86% with tokenized input to 16-34% with visual grids. That also argues against Lee-style map-as-image tools for the numeric arms.

Implication 6 (unique tag IDs trivialise data association) is a sound inference, and it is the strongest design insight. It should be tested, though: no source covers LLM behaviour with aliased beacons.

The unknowns list says there are no benchmark results for the named models. That is true, but it omits that the models themselves are real and very new, released in September 2026. The benchmark design should therefore assume no prior spatial evals exist and plan for API version drift.
missed: The named frontier models exist and are very recent. GPT-6 Astra had a limited preview on 2026-09-03 and API pricing of $10/$50 per million input/output tokens, per a search snippet from https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/ and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPT-6_Astra. GPT-6 Sol (with Luna) launched on 2026-09-22 (https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/22/openai-launches-gpt-6-sol-and-luna/). Claude Fable 5.1 launched on 2026-09-01; its announcement mentions 'fewer confident wrong answers' (search snippet, https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/09/claude-fable-5-1-aws/). No published spatial or SLAM evaluations exist for them yet.

Lee 2026 gives the LLM the occupancy map as a rendered image through MCP tools named subscribe_map_as_image, draw_map_axis, draw_robot_pose, write_semantic_data and get_semantic_data. The LLM picks waypoints 'toward the largest unexplored area' by looking at the image, and no latency is reported (https://arxiv.org/html/2609.27340v1). This is a concrete tool-interface template, and write_semantic_data (natural-language landmark description plus pose) maps directly onto a beacon log.
Aitha 2026's occupancy map comes from an RGB-D depth image converted with depthimage_to_laserscan, so its frontier method needs depth hardware this robot lacks (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.23165v1).

VLG-Loc requires a known 'labeled footprint map', so it is localization in a known map, not SLAM in an unknown one. It was validated in simulated and real retail environments (https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12793).

Sandfuchs 2026 tested open-weight models relevant to the local-model arm (Gemma-3-27B-Instruct, Qwen3-235B, QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1, Llama-3.3-70B, Mistral-Large, GPT-OSS-120B). Reasoning-tuned models, including GPT-OSS-120B, reached 100% while instruct-tuned dense models 'largely failed at navigation' (https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09604v1). This is the closest evidence for how the local Qwen and Gemma models might fare.

Lost in Aggregation's delegation gain (up to +92 pp) 'diminished at larger scales (30×30)', so tool delegation is not a complete fix as the map grows (https://arxiv.org/html/2606.22219). LLM-MapRepair shares authors with it (Jiang, Meng).

RoboAtlas ran on a real Unitree Go2 over areas larger than 1800 m2 with about 30k semantic instances, using OpenRoboVox mapping. It is real-world Active SLAM with VLM arms, not simulation only (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26046).
ConceptGraphs' real-robot poses came from Open3D SLAM (LiDAR) and RTAB-Map, and its LLM also infers inter-object relation edges (https://arxiv.org/html/2309.16650v1).
STI-Bench's best model is Gemini-2.5-Pro at 41.4% (https://mint-sjtu.github.io/STI-Bench.io/).

ROVER notes that the LLM-assisted loop-closure method also fails in 'scenes without textual information' (https://arxiv.org/html/2508.13488v1). That is relevant if loop closure has to work from ESP32-CAM images with tags hidden.

I also searched for published work on LLMs doing in-context Kalman-filter or landmark-SLAM estimation with ATE, on VLMs decoding AprilTag IDs, and on LLM agents calling GTSAM or g2o as a tool, and found nothing. The researcher's unknowns hold. The nearest hits were LLMs used to discover Kalman-filter variants (arXiv:2508.11703), which is algorithm search, not estimation.

research.summary: Classical fiducial SLAM is a mature, well-supported baseline for this robot. TagSLAM (Pfrommer & Daniilidis 2019, arXiv:1910.00679) is a GTSAM front end that uses AprilTags and optional odometry. It has a ROS 2 branch, still marked "work in progress", that needs Jazzy or newer. The same design is easy to hand-build with GTSAM's planar SLAM factors, or as an EKF-SLAM with known correspondence. Unique tag IDs largely remove the data-association problem: TagSLAM says loop closure is "guaranteed once a tag is successfully decoded". The risks that remain are wrong loop closures from human error (duplicate IDs, wrong tag size) and pose ambiguity. On accuracy, no source gives numbers for an ESP32-CAM/OV3660, but close analogues show how things scale. A 1080p webcam with 15 cm markers gave about 3–5 cm RMSE from a single marker at 1.3 m, about 30–45 cm at 3 m, and about 4 cm when 5 or more markers were visible (Hinderer et al. 2025). A single AprilTag at 70 cm gave about 4.4 cm raw x-error (Abbas et al. 2019). A Duckiebot EKF-SLAM with no wheel encoders had about 0.25 m mean landmark error, and did better when it used only tags closer than 90 cm (SLAMDuck). The camera link is the tightest limit. An OV2640 ESP32-CAM streaming over HTTP reached about 14 fps at 640x480 and about 8 fps at 800x600; OV3660 users report roughly 15 fps at most, with latency around 80 ms or more. The software runs on the Spark's aarch64: apriltag_ros, GTSAM, image_proc and camera_calibration all have arm64 ROS 2 Jazzy binaries, GTSAM 4.3.0 also has aarch64 PyPI wheels, and isaac_ros_apriltag officially supports DGX Spark, but only on ROS 2 Lyrical. Overall, a classical tag-SLAM should plausibly reach map and trajectory errors of several centimetres up to a few decimetres in a small arena. That makes it a meaningful reference for an LLM estimator, but the exact number has to be measured on this hardware rather than assumed.

claims.claim: TagSLAM (Bernd Pfrommer, Kostas Daniilidis, 2019, arXiv:1910.00679, 'TagSLAM: Robust SLAM with Fiducial Markers') is a ROS front end to the GTSAM factor-graph optimizer for SLAM with AprilTags.
claims.quote: TagSLAM provides a convenient, flexible, and robust way of performing Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) with AprilTag fiducial markers.

claims.claim: TagSLAM paper: with fiducials, loop closure becomes trivial once a tag ID is decoded. The unique-ID property removes the landmark recognition problem.
claims.quote: loop closure is guaranteed once a tag is successfully decoded by the AprilTag library. If one or more tags are visible at all times, then TagSLAM can perform both tracking and loop closure.

claims.claim: TagSLAM paper: localizing from one small tag is unreliable because of pose ambiguity; one tag is only satisfactory together with odometry or when the tag appears large in the image.
claims.quote: a tag corner error of just a single pixel can lead to a dramatically different pose initialization. Localizing off of a single tag is therefore intrinsically difficult, and should be avoided. Satisfactory results from a single tag can only be expected in combination with odometry input or when the tag image is sufficiently large.

claims.claim: TagSLAM paper: ambiguity is worst when a tag is viewed nearly face-on, so TagSLAM gates new tag poses by an ambiguity ratio and viewing angle.
claims.quote: tag pose ambiguity is most serious a problem when the tag is seen at a small angle

claims.claim: TagSLAM paper: human input errors (duplicate IDs, wrong printed tag size) are a frequent root cause of failure.
claims.quote: human errors are frequently the root cause, such as inaccuracies or outright typos when entering measured tag poses, intrinsic or extrinsic calibration errors, duplicate tag ids, errors in tag size due to printing or misspecfication

claims.claim: The TagSLAM paper reports no quantitative position-error numbers. Its demo (630 m, 57 tags) shows loop closure only qualitatively, and it reports runtime: about 12 ms/frame on average on an i9, with spikes up to 260 ms as the graph grows.
claims.quote: which is an average performance of about 12ms per frame ... individual frames can take as much as 260ms

claims.claim: The TagSLAM ROS 2 port is on the 'ros2' branch (the default branch). It is marked work-in-progress, needs Jazzy or newer, and optionally takes odometry.
claims.quote: ROS2 is WORK IN PROGRESS. Documentation will follow. ... At the moment TagSLAM requires ROS2 Rolling/Jazzy or newer. ... TagSLAM operates off of tags (and odometry messages, if provided).

claims.claim: UcoSLAM (Rafael Munoz-Salinas, Rafael Medina-Carnicer, 2019, arXiv:1902.03729) fuses keypoints and square fiducial markers. It reports that the combination beats either one alone, but the abstract gives no numbers.
claims.quote: Our tests also show that the combination of markers and keypoints achieves better accuracy than each one of them independently.

claims.claim: EKF-SLAM in its textbook form assumes known correspondence and a range-bearing sensor. Wrong loop closures make it diverge, and it scales poorly to large maps.
claims.quote: Assumption: known correspondence ... Range-bearing sensor ... Known data association ... Wrong loop closures lead to filter divergence ... The EKF becomes computationally intractable for large maps!

claims.claim: GTSAM's Planar SLAM example (Pose2 poses, Point2 landmarks, BetweenFactor odometry, BearingRangeFactor observations, one unique key per landmark) is the standard template for 2D landmark SLAM.
claims.quote: 'True' Simultaneous Localization and Mapping optimizes for both the unknown robot trajectory and unknown landmarks.

claims.claim: MathWorks' AprilTag landmark-SLAM example states outright that tag IDs remove most of the data-association burden.
claims.quote: By using fiducial markers like AprilTags, the block pattern in the image provides unique IDs for each landmark observation. This ID information reduces the need for difficult data association algorithms.

claims.claim: SLAMDuck is the closest analogue to this robot: a small differential-drive robot with a monocular camera running EKF-SLAM on AprilTag range-bearing, with no encoders (commanded wheel velocities only). It got about 0.25 m mean landmark error against Vicon, and improved when it kept only tags closer than 90 cm.
claims.quote: our landmark positions are far from the ground truth position with average errors in the x and y directions of -0.27 m and -0.23 m respectively ... only considering range measurements that are less than 90 cm away ... Possible improvements to our experiment could entail installing wheel encoders to the system.

claims.claim: Duckietown's EKF-SLAM write-up lists AprilTag failure modes on small robots: lighting, ambiguity at shallow angles, and non-Gaussian errors.
claims.quote: AprilTag detection is constrained by lighting artifacts and pose ambiguity at shallow viewing angles

claims.claim: AprilTag 1 (Edwin Olson, 2011, 'AprilTag: A robust and flexible visual fiducial system', ICRA): localization accuracy is driven by the tag's apparent size, which depends on distance and angle. The accuracy experiments were synthetic (400x400 ray-traced images), and real-world accuracy will be worse.
claims.quote: The main factor in localization accuracy is the size of the target, which is affected by both the distance and orientation of the tag. ... Naturally, real-world performance of the system will be lower than these synthetic experiments due to noise, lighting variation, and other non-idealities (such as lens distortion or tag non-planarity).

claims.claim: AprilTag 2 (John Wang, Edwin Olson, IROS 2016, 'AprilTag 2: Efficient and robust fiducial detection'): decimated images keep localization accuracy while detection gets much faster. Real-image tests used 1296x964 pixels and 0.167 m tags at 0.6–7.0 m. The numeric errors appear only in plots.
claims.quote: The new detector vastly outperforms the old detector when decimated images are used, without noticeably affecting localization accuracy vs. non-decimated images. ... Images were taken with a Point Grey Chameleon at 1296 x 964 pixels, and each tag is 0.167m wide.

claims.claim: AprilTag 3 (Maximilian Krogius, Acshi Haggenmiller, Edwin Olson, IROS 2019, 'Flexible Layouts for Fiducial Tags'): the detector is faster and has higher recall than AprilTag 2 and ArUco, and the main tradeoff is small-tag recall versus speed. The 36h11 family has 587 unique IDs.
claims.quote: We can see that the AprilTag 3 detector is faster and has higher recall than both the AprilTag 2 and ArUco detectors. ... The main tradeoff in a fiducial detector is between recall, particularly of small tags, and speed. ... the old maki 36h11 family ... is 10x10 cells in size and has only 587 tags.

claims.claim: AprilTag library README: raising quad_decimate trades detection distance for speed. Tag size must be measured at the black/white border boundary, not the outer edge; getting this wrong scales every range.
claims.quote: Increasing the quad_decimate parameter will increase the speed of the detector at the cost of detection distance. ... Note: The tag size should not be measured from the outside of the tag.

claims.claim: Abbas et al. (Sensors 2019, 'Analysis and Improvements in AprilTag Based State Estimation'): raw single-AprilTag error at 70 cm was 4.4 cm in x and 2.56 cm in y. Camera yaw relative to the tag is the dominant error source.
claims.quote: the angular rotation of the camera (yaw angle) about its vertical axis is the primary source of error that decreases the precision to the point where the marker system is not potentially viable for sub-decimeter precise tasks ... we have improved the accuracy from 4.4 cm to 0.8 cm in the x-axis and 2.56 cm to 0.54 cm in the y-axis

claims.claim: Hinderer, Scheffler, Yang (arXiv:2509.17345, 2025, 'Investigation of ArUco Marker Placement for Planar Indoor Localization') used a 1080p Logitech C920 and 15 cm markers. Single-marker planar localization RMSE was 2.75 cm (x), 5.16 cm (y) and 0.36° at a camera-marker distance of 1.334 m, but 45.29 cm, 31.38 cm and 1.04° at 2.991 m.
claims.quote: The camera is a Logitech C920 Pro HD with a resolution of 1080p ... printed with a square marker size of (15, 15) cm. [Table II, All:] 2.75 5.16 0.36 [Table III, All:] 45.29 31.38 1.04

claims.claim: Hinderer et al. 2025: at 2.991 m, error falls steeply as more markers are visible (1 marker: 45.29/31.38 cm, 3: 8.83/8.81 cm, 5: 3.72/4.59 cm). The authors recommend 5 or more visible markers and note ambiguity when a marker is seen face-on.
claims.quote: markers should be placed such that 5+ markers must be visible from every feasible AMR position if high reliability is required ... camera pose ambiguity during frontal observation of the marker

claims.claim: Ch'ng et al. (arXiv:1909.11888, 2019, 'Resolving Marker Pose Ambiguity by Robust Rotation Averaging with Clique Constraints'): single-marker planar pose estimation is fundamentally ambiguous, especially with noisy corners.
claims.quote: PPE suffers from a fundamental ambiguity problem, in that there can be more than one plausible pose solutions for a PPE instance. Especially when localisation of the marker corners is noisy, it is often difficult to disambiguate the pose solutions based on reprojection error alone.

claims.claim: The Espressif esp32-camera driver supports the OV3660 up to 2048x1536. JPEG above CIF needs PSRAM, and multiple frame buffers raise frame rate at the cost of memory and CPU.
claims.quote: Except when using CIF or lower resolution with JPEG, the driver requires PSRAM to be installed and activated.

claims.claim: OV3660 users on the esp32-camera tracker report low frame rates: about 15 fps maximum across sizes on one board.
claims.quote: Currently, max fps is around 15fps. I have tried whole sizes.

claims.claim: ESP32-CAM benchmark (Nowroz et al., arXiv:2505.24081, 2025, 'A Benchmark Reference for ESP32-CAM Module') covers the OV2640, not the OV3660, streaming over HTTP from the Arduino CameraServer. Measured averages: 14.19 fps at 640x480 (~15.6 KB/frame), 8.25 fps at 800x600 (~27 KB/frame), 3.37 fps at 1024x768. The paper's text elsewhere says VGA drops 'below 10 FPS', which contradicts its own table.
claims.quote: 640x480 14.19 71.25 15572.34 / 800x600 8.25 72.34 26978.11 / 1024x768 3.37 ... Performance begins to degrade noticeably beyond this point, dropping below 10 FPS at 640×480

claims.claim: Custom raw-Wi-Fi-injection firmware (not HTTP) reaches much higher ESP32-CAM rates and lower latency, which shows the stock HTTP server is a large part of the bottleneck.
claims.quote: 34-44 FPS at 800x600 or 640x480 with 50-80ms latency

claims.claim: A 2025/2026 Springer chapter (seen only as a search snippet) reports about 78 ms median latency for an ESP32-S3 with OV2640 sending JPEG over Wi-Fi through micro-ROS to a ROS 2 host. Most of the delay is encoding, serialization and wireless transmission.
claims.quote: most latency arises during image encoding, serialization, and wireless transmission, with a median delay of approximately 78 ms

claims.claim: AprilTag detection has been run on the ESP32 itself (apriltag-esp32). 5 cm 36h11 tags are detected from beyond 1.5 m at SVGA, at 100–200 ms/frame with pose. The library limits the 36h11 family to 35 tags because of memory.
claims.quote: 5cm, square 36h11 tags can be detected from > 1.5M ... 200ms (2 threads) in SVGA resolution, 150ms (single-thread) in VGA resolution and under 100ms (single-thread) in HVGA resolution ... VGA also works great but might not suitable for small tags ... currently to 35 tags for each of these family

claims.claim: apriltag_ros (ROS 2, Christian Rauch) takes rectified images, raw or compressed transport, plus camera_info. It publishes tag poses on /tf and detections with hamming distance and decision_margin. Version 3.4.0 is released for Humble, Jazzy, Kilted, Lyrical and Rolling.
claims.quote: The node subscribes via a `image_transport::CameraSubscriber` to rectified images on topic `image_rect`. ... `image_rect/compressed` (`compressed`, type: `sensor_msgs/msg/CompressedImage`)

claims.claim: The official ROS 2 arm64 (aarch64) apt index for Ubuntu Noble contains Jazzy binaries of apriltag_ros, apriltag, gtsam, image_proc, camera_calibration, robot_localization and slam_toolbox.
claims.quote: Package: ros-jazzy-apriltag-ros Version: 3.4.0-1noble.20260903.041558 ... Package: ros-jazzy-gtsam Version: 4.2.0-4noble.20260306.121241 ... Package: ros-jazzy-image-proc

claims.claim: REP 2000 lists ROS 2 Jazzy on Ubuntu Noble arm64 as Tier 1, with Debian packages provided.
claims.quote: |    arm64     | Tier 1 [d][a][s] |

claims.claim: isaac_ros_apriltag officially supports DGX Spark, but only with ROS 2 Lyrical and DGX OS 7.2.3. It needs rectified input and offers CUDA and CPU backends.
claims.quote: This package is designed and tested to be compatible with ROS 2 Lyrical running on Jetson, an x86_64 system with an NVIDIA GPU, or a DGX Spark workstation.

claims.claim: GTSAM 4.3.0 on PyPI ships prebuilt Linux aarch64 wheels, so a Python factor-graph baseline installs directly on the Spark.
claims.quote: gtsam-4.3.0-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_27_aarch64.manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl

claims.claim: Borenstein & Feng (IEEE T-RA 1996): differential-drive odometry error is dominated by wheelbase uncertainty and unequal wheel diameters. Calibration improves accuracy by at least 10x, but uncorrected odometry becomes useless within about 10 m.
claims.quote: Typical odometry errors will become so large that the robot's internal position estimate is totally wrong after as little as 10 m of travel [Gourley and Trivedi, 1994].

claims.claim: The BNO055 has a 6-axis IMU fusion mode (IMUPLUS) that uses only the accelerometer and gyroscope. It gives relative orientation with no magnetometer, which sidesteps motor magnetic interference.
claims.quote: In the IMU mode the relative orientation of the BNO055 in space is calculated from the accelerometer and gyroscope data. The calculation is fast (i.e. high output data rate).

claims.claim: The standard SLAM metrics are ATE (global consistency after alignment) and RPE (drift). The evo tool computes both (APE/RPE) directly from ROS 2 bags.
claims.quote: The absolute trajectory error directly measures the difference between points of the true and the estimated trajectory. ... This script computes the error in the relative motion between pairs of timestamps.

claims.claim: evo is a Python package for evaluating odometry and SLAM trajectories, and it reads ROS and ROS 2 bag files.
claims.quote: Python package for the evaluation of odometry and SLAM

claims.claim: Duckietown Autolab (Tani et al., arXiv:2009.04362, 2020) gets low-cost real-world ground truth from fixed 'Watchtower' cameras. They detect AprilTags on the robots and on the map, and fuse them with a g2o pose graph.
claims.quote: The localization system comprises a network of Watchtowers, i.e., low-cost observation structures using the same sensing and computation as the Duckiebots. ... A set of calibration AprilTags are fixed to the road layer of the map

implications: INFERENCE (feasibility): The fixed hardware supports a classical landmark-SLAM baseline. Compute is not the limit; the limits are the camera (resolution × frame rate × latency over 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi) and the odometry. Aim for a baseline in the 'several cm to a few dm' range in a small arena, not mm-level. No source measures this exact camera, so the baseline error must be measured on the real robot and written into the benchmark as the reference.

INFERENCE (recommended classical baseline, B1): a hand-written Python GTSAM planar factor graph. Pose2 per keyframe; one Point2 landmark per AprilTag, keyed by tag ID; BetweenFactor from encoder odometry, with yaw from the BNO055 in IMUPLUS mode (no magnetometer); BearingRangeFactor from each apriltag_ros detection, using only the tag-centre translation turned into range and bearing (with the camera extrinsic). Solve with iSAM2 online and a full batch at the end. This is short, fully inspectable, uses the same inputs the LLM sees, and installs from the aarch64 PyPI wheel or ros-jazzy-gtsam.

INFERENCE (secondary baselines): (B0) dead-reckoning only, the lower bound. (B2) EKF-SLAM with known correspondence, the didactic textbook version. (B3) TagSLAM ROS 2, an independent off-the-shelf reference; its ROS 2 port is marked WIP, so budget time or treat it as optional. A good LLM should fall between B0 and B1. Beating B0 is the minimum success criterion; approaching B1 would be strong.

INFERENCE (camera pipeline): ESP32-CAM JPEG at VGA (about 10–15 fps expected, from the OV2640 data plus OV3660 anecdotes) → a small HTTP/MJPEG-to-ROS bridge publishing CompressedImage with timestamps → image_proc rectification, using intrinsics from ros-jazzy-camera-calibration → apriltag_ros with the CPU backend. isaac_ros_apriltag is unnecessary at these frame rates, and it only officially supports ROS 2 Lyrical on DGX OS 7.2.3; check which ROS 2 distro the Spark actually runs.

INFERENCE (stop-and-look protocol): with roughly 80–150 ms latency, ~10 fps, motion blur and TT-motor backlash, the robot should stop after each bounded move and collect N frames (e.g. 5) while stationary. It then averages the detections per tag and hands one observation set to both the classical estimator and the LLM. This also fits naturally with LLM turn-taking and makes the two estimators get identical evidence.

INFERENCE (tag sizing): apriltag-esp32 detects a 5 cm tag at over 1.5 m at 800 px wide, so detection starts at roughly 20 px across the tag. At 640 px wide, with an assumed ~60–65° horizontal FOV (the real FOV of this OV3660 module is unknown), a 15 cm tag is about 38 px at 2 m and about 25 px at 3 m. That is detectable, but pose/range quality will be poor, given Hinderer's 30–45 cm single-marker RMSE at 3 m with 1080p. Recommendation: tags of at least 15–20 cm (measured at the black/white border), mostly used within about 2 m, and density such that 2–3 or more tags are usually in view.

INFERENCE (ambiguity mitigation): for a ground robot, constrain the estimate to SE(2) (fixed camera height, roll and pitch). Use tag translation (range, bearing) rather than inverting the full tag rotation, because a rotation flip gets amplified by the lever arm into large position error. Gate out detections with low decision_margin, hamming>0, very small pixel area, or near-frontal small tags, following TagSLAM's ambiguity gate. Mount tags vertically at camera height on varied walls or stands.

INFERENCE (data association and benchmark design): unique 36h11 IDs make data association and loop closure trivial for both classical and LLM estimators. With IDs given, the benchmark mainly tests metric fusion (odometry plus noisy range-bearing), which is exactly where LLMs are expected to be weakest. To test 'recognising revisits', add conditions such as: (a) IDs hidden, where the model gets 'a tag' plus geometry only, or a VLM must read the raw image; (b) a few deliberately duplicated IDs; (c) raw JPEG frames with no detector at all, for VLM/VLA tracks.

INFERENCE (odometry): 4320 counts/rev (x4) gives far more resolution than needed. Systematic errors (unequal wheel diameter, effective wheelbase) will dominate, so run a UMBmark-style square-path calibration before collecting any benchmark data. Use BNO055 IMUPLUS (gyro-only) yaw to avoid the motor-magnet problem on the compass.

INFERENCE (ground truth): in simulation (Gazebo Harmonic / Isaac Sim), use exact simulator poses and tag positions. In the real world, measure tag positions by hand (tape/laser) as the map ground truth, following TagSLAM's use of laser-measured tags. For trajectory ground truth, use a Duckietown-style overhead 'watchtower' webcam that tracks one or more AprilTags on the robot's roof, mounted low (about 1.3–2 m) or with several roof tags. Hinderer shows a single marker at 3 m is not good enough for ground truth.

INFERENCE (metrics): report ATE and RPE (via evo from ROS 2 bags), landmark-map RMSE after SE(2)/Umeyama alignment keyed by tag ID, loop-closure correctness, number of lost/diverged runs, per-step decision latency, and token/$ cost. Report each LLM relative to B0 and B1 on identical logged observation sequences. Replaying the same logged bags to every model makes the comparison fair and repeatable, and offline replay makes the many-model comparison cheap.

INFERENCE (risks): the ESP32-CAM and Pico 2 W micro-ROS share the 2.4 GHz band, so expect latency spikes. OV3660 driver frame-rate issues are reported. JPEG above CIF needs PSRAM. A wrong printed tag size scales every range. Lighting and motion blur cause missed detections. The TagSLAM ROS 2 port is WIP. None of these threaten feasibility; all argue for stop-and-look operation and offline bag replay.

INFERENCE (optional variant): run AprilTag detection on the ESP32 itself (apriltag-esp32) and send only IDs and corners. This cuts bandwidth and latency, but the rate is limited to about 5–10 Hz, the family is limited to 35 36h11 IDs, and it uses the camera MCU's memory. It is worth trying only if Wi-Fi JPEG streaming turns out to be the bottleneck.
unknowns: No published measurement of OV3660 (as opposed to OV2640) ESP32-CAM JPEG frame rate and end-to-end latency at VGA/SVGA over HTTP. The only OV3660 evidence is anecdotal GitHub issues (~15 fps max).

No published AprilTag pose/range accuracy study using an ESP32-CAM or OV3660 image stream. The accuracy numbers above come from 1080p webcams (Hinderer), unspecified cameras (Abbas), or synthetic/industrial cameras (Olson, Wang).
The field of view, lens distortion and rolling-shutter behaviour of the specific OV3660 module (needed to predict tag pixel size and motion blur) were not found.

The TagSLAM paper reports no quantitative trajectory/map error. The UcoSLAM and SPM-SLAM accuracy numbers, and the Kalaitzakis et al. (2021 JINT) AprilTag error tables, were not retrieved because they are paywalled or only abstracts were accessible.
The AprilTag 2 paper's position-error-vs-distance and orientation-error-vs-angle numbers are only in plots and could not be extracted as exact values.
The ~78 ms ESP32-S3/OV2640 micro-ROS latency figure comes from a search snippet only; the Springer chapter itself could not be fetched.
Which ROS 2 distribution is installed on the user's DGX Spark (this decides whether isaac_ros_apriltag, which needs Lyrical, applies; apriltag_ros binaries exist for Jazzy arm64).
BNO055 IMUPLUS gyro yaw drift rate on this robot, and how badly motor fields affect NDOF mode, were not quantified.
TT gear-motor odometry accuracy (backlash, slip, wheel-diameter mismatch) was not found in any source; it must be measured (e.g. UMBmark).
