Whether 2.4 GHz contention between the ESP32-CAM stream and Pico 2 W micro-ROS traffic causes latency spikes large enough to matter was not investigated.
Whether the MathWorks and gtbook quotes are exactly verbatim: they came through a summarizing fetch tool (marked medium confidence).

verdicts.claim: TagSLAM (Pfrommer & Daniilidis, 2019, arXiv:1910.00679) is a ROS front end to GTSAM for SLAM with AprilTags.
verdicts.note: The PDF says: 'TagSLAM provides a front end to the GTSAM factor graph optimizer that makes it possible to rapidly design a range of experiments'.

verdicts.claim: TagSLAM: loop closure is guaranteed once a tag is decoded, so unique IDs remove the landmark-recognition problem.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim. The paper frames this for scenes with few landmarks ('fewer than 100'). It says decoding makes recognition trivial, not that the geometry is right.

verdicts.claim: TagSLAM: localizing from a single small tag is unreliable; it is satisfactory only with odometry or when the tag appears large.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim. The preceding clause matters: 'For a tag that is barely large enough to be detected and is viewed at a shallow angle, a tag corner error of just a single pixel...'

verdicts.claim: TagSLAM: ambiguity is worst when a tag is viewed nearly face-on, so TagSLAM gates new tag poses by ambiguity ratio and viewing angle.
verdicts.note: The quote exists. But 'nearly face-on' is the researcher's reading, not TagSLAM's wording. The same paper calls the hard case a tag 'viewed at a shallow angle'. The gate is 'e(γ)/e(γ̇) > 0.3 while being viewed at an angle of less than 60°', and the angle convention is ambiguous. The Duckietown blog also says 'pose ambiguity at shallow viewing angles'. Frontal ambiguity is supported by Hinderer ('camera pose ambiguity during frontal observation') and Ch'ng, but not by this TagSLAM quote.

verdicts.claim: TagSLAM: human input errors (duplicate IDs, wrong tag size) are a frequent root cause of failure.
verdicts.note: Verbatim. The list also includes 'using tags that are not planar, or supplying unsychronized stereo images'.

verdicts.claim: The TagSLAM paper has no quantitative position-error numbers; the demo (630 m, 57 tags) is qualitative; about 12 ms/frame on an i9, up to 260 ms.
verdicts.note: Confirmed: the application section compares trajectories only in a figure. The researcher omits that the 57 tag poses were 'deterimined from the wall orientations and from laser distance measurements with a Leica Disto D3a', and that the odometry was stereo VIO. So the demo is loop closure against a surveyed tag map, not unknown-map SLAM.

verdicts.claim: The TagSLAM ROS 2 port is on the 'ros2' branch (default), is work-in-progress, needs Jazzy or newer, and takes optional odometry.
verdicts.note: README: 'ROS2 is WORK IN PROGRESS. Documentation will follow.' and 'requires ROS2 Rolling/Jazzy or newer'. The GitHub API shows default_branch=ros2, last pushed 2026-01-08.

verdicts.claim: UcoSLAM (Munoz-Salinas & Medina-Carnicer, 2019, arXiv:1902.03729): markers plus keypoints beat either alone; no numbers in the abstract.
verdicts.note: The abstract sentence is verbatim; submitted 11 Feb 2019.

verdicts.claim: Textbook EKF-SLAM assumes known correspondence and a range-bearing sensor; wrong loop closures cause divergence; it scales poorly.
verdicts.note: All the phrases appear in the slides. The slides also say it 'Can diverge if non-linearities are large'.

verdicts.claim: GTSAM Planar SLAM example (Pose2, Point2, BetweenFactor, BearingRangeFactor) is the standard 2D landmark-SLAM template.
verdicts.note: Re-fetched. The quote is present, and the code uses PriorFactorPose2, BetweenFactorPose2 and BearingRangeFactor2D. 'Standard template' is a mild characterisation.

verdicts.claim: MathWorks AprilTag landmark-SLAM example: tag IDs reduce the need for data-association algorithms.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim. It uses real data: an Axis M1013 camera at 640x480 plus Jackal odometry. It reports only differences between two optimizers (sub-mm), not accuracy against ground truth.

verdicts.claim: SLAMDuck: EKF-SLAM on a Duckiebot with AprilTag range-bearing and no encoders; ~0.25 m mean landmark error against Vicon; improved using only tags <90 cm.
verdicts.note: -0.27 m / -0.23 m are signed average x/y errors (bias), not a mean error magnitude. The trajectory was 'much bigger' than ground truth. With the 90 cm cutoff, the README says x/y pose errors got smaller but 'we see a decreased performance in our heading estimates', and gives no landmark numbers. This is an unreviewed student-project README. The no-encoder part is supported ('Possible improvements ... installing wheel encoders').

verdicts.claim: Duckietown EKF-SLAM blog lists AprilTag failure modes: lighting, ambiguity at shallow angles, non-Gaussian errors.
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'AprilTag detection is constrained by lighting artifacts and pose ambiguity at shallow viewing angles, introducing non-Gaussian errors'. Authors are Zamani, Oest O'Leary and Lessard, 2025-04-26. No accuracy numbers. Note it says 'shallow', which conflicts with the researcher's 'face-on' framing.

verdicts.claim: AprilTag 1 (Olson 2011): accuracy is driven by apparent tag size; experiments were synthetic 400x400; real-world will be worse.
verdicts.note: Both sentences are verbatim; images were 'generated at a resolution of 400 × 400 with a pinhole lens and focal length of 400 pixels'.

verdicts.claim: AprilTag 2 (Wang & Olson, IROS 2016): decimation keeps accuracy while detection gets faster; real tests used 1296x964 images and 0.167 m tags at 0.6–7.0 m.
verdicts.note: Verbatim. The real-image test aligned the camera with the centre tag, moved it perpendicularly away (a frontal geometry), and rectified before detection. Laser tape was the ground truth.

verdicts.claim: AprilTag 3 (Krogius, Haggenmiller, Olson, IROS 2019): faster and higher recall than AprilTag 2 and ArUco; small-tag recall vs speed tradeoff; 36h11 has 587 IDs.
verdicts.note: All three quotes are verbatim.

verdicts.claim: AprilTag README: quad_decimate trades distance for speed; tag size is measured at the black/white border boundary.
verdicts.note: Verbatim. The README also points to OpenCV SOLVEPNP_IPPE_SQUARE as an alternative pose solver.

verdicts.claim: Abbas et al. (Sensors 2019): raw single-tag error at 70 cm was 4.4 cm x / 2.56 cm y; camera yaw is the dominant error source.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim (Sensors 2019, 19, 5480), but the figure is qualified 'in an ideal scenario'. The same sentence gives raw precision (variance) of 112 cm² in x, a standard deviation of about 10.6 cm, at 70 cm. So raw single-tag scatter is much larger than the 4.4 cm accuracy figure suggests.

verdicts.claim: Hinderer, Scheffler, Yang (arXiv:2509.17345, 2025): C920 1080p, 15 cm markers; single-marker RMSE 2.75/5.16 cm at 1.334 m and 45.29/31.38 cm at 2.991 m.
verdicts.note: The numbers match Tables II/III. Caveats the researcher understates: (1) the markers are ArUco DICT_6X6_1000, not AprilTag; (2) the camera is taped to the ceiling looking straight down at floor markers, a frontal geometry and the worst ambiguity case, unlike a forward camera viewing wall tags; (3) the 'distance' is the camera height, and the Table II caption says 1.344 m while the text says 1.334 m.

verdicts.claim: Hinderer 2025: at 2.991 m error falls steeply with more visible markers (1: 45/31 cm, 3: 8.8/8.8, 5: 3.7/4.6); recommends 5+ markers; frontal ambiguity.
verdicts.note: Table IV and both quotes verified. The paper also notes 'maximum errors can be larger with more markers' and a systematic calibration error that 'does not decrease by adding markers'.

verdicts.claim: Ch'ng et al. (arXiv:1909.11888, 2019): single-marker planar pose estimation is fundamentally ambiguous, especially with noisy corners.
verdicts.note: Verbatim. First author Shin-Fang Ch'ng.

verdicts.claim: esp32-camera supports OV3660 up to 2048x1536; JPEG above CIF needs PSRAM; multiple frame buffers raise frame rate at a memory/CPU cost.
verdicts.note: The README table lists 'OV3660 | 2048 x 1536'. PSRAM sentence verbatim. Two or more frame buffers 'allows for double the frame rate. Please use only with JPEG.'

verdicts.claim: OV3660 users report ~15 fps max across sizes.
verdicts.note: This is one user, on a custom board with 4 MB PSRAM. The issue was closed 2020-12-29 and is six years old, anecdotal and possibly outdated. 'Users' (plural) overstates it.

verdicts.claim: Nowroz et al. (arXiv:2505.24081, 2025): OV2640 over HTTP (CameraServer); 14.19 fps at 640x480, 8.25 at 800x600, 3.37 at 1024x768; the text contradicts the table.
verdicts.note: The table values and the 'dropping below 10 FPS at 640×480' contradiction are both verified. The FPS is logged on the device, and no end-to-end latency was measured. The chip ran at about 70–74 °C.

verdicts.claim: esp32-cam-fpv raw Wi-Fi injection reaches 34–44 fps at 640x480/800x600 with 50–80 ms latency, showing the HTTP server is a large part of the bottleneck.
verdicts.note: The numbers are verbatim. It uses an OV2640, a modified camera driver that streams from DMA, FEC, and packet injection to a Raspberry Pi receiver with Wi-Fi cards in monitor mode; the author calls it 'very WIP'. It changes several things at once, so it does not isolate HTTP as the bottleneck. It also cannot share a normal AP/station network with the Pico's micro-ROS link.

verdicts.claim: Springer chapter: ~78 ms median latency for ESP32-S3 + OV2640 JPEG via micro-ROS to a ROS 2 host.
verdicts.note: Snippet only; the page redirects to a Springer login. Title: 'Timing Analysis of Low-Cost Edge Vision for Object Detection for Smart Factory Systems'. The resolution for the 78 ms figure is unknown, and the chip is an ESP32-S3, not an ESP32 with an OV3660. Keep as low confidence.

verdicts.claim: apriltag-esp32: 5 cm 36h11 tags detected beyond 1.5 m at SVGA; 100–200 ms/frame with pose; limited to 35 tags per family.
verdicts.note: The cited URL (branch 'main') returns 404; the default branch is 'master', where the quotes are verbatim. The distance is under 'Max distance: to be tested ... might even be further, but haven't tested', so it is a lower bound, not a measured limit. The 35-tag limit can be changed ('You may modify the number').

implication_challenges: 'Several cm to a few dm' baseline: the sources don't carry over to this robot. Hinderer uses 1080p ArUco looking straight down from the ceiling; Abbas's 4.4 cm is an 'ideal scenario' with a raw variance of 112 cm²; SLAMDuck's figures are signed biases in a student README. A rough pixel-scaling INFERENCE: 640 px is about 3x fewer pixels per axis than 1080p, so Hinderer's single-marker 1.33 m case (3–5 cm) maps to roughly 0.45 m at VGA, and the 3 m case (30–45 cm) to roughly 1 m, if the fields of view are similar. The low end of the range is optimistic for single-tag views beyond about 1 m.

Tag sizing (about 20 px detection threshold; use tags within about 2 m): the 20 px figure comes from apriltag-esp32's '>1.5M ... might even be further, but haven't tested'. That is a lower bound on range, not a detection threshold. The FOV used for the conversion is also assumed. Scaling Hinderer as above, 2 m single-tag ranging at VGA would likely be decimetre-level, not a comfortable working range. Recommend measuring range error against distance on the real camera before fixing the tag layout.

Ambiguity mitigation 'following TagSLAM's ambiguity gate': apriltag_ros publishes only the homography, hamming and decision_margin, not the two-solution pose-ambiguity error that TagSLAM gates on. Copying the gate needs a custom detector wrapper (for example apriltag's estimate_tag_pose, which returns err, or IPPE). The sources also disagree on where ambiguity is worst: TagSLAM and Duckietown say 'shallow angle', Hinderer and Ch'ng say frontal. The gating rule should be tested, not assumed.

'A good LLM should fall between B0 and B1': no source supports this expectation. An LLM doing metric fusion could plausibly do worse than dead-reckoning (B0). Present it as a hypothesis for the benchmark to test, not a prior.

Offline bag replay as the main many-model comparison: replay tests only the estimation part. The project also wants the LLM to 'decide where to explore next'. That is closed-loop, so every model's choices change what it observes, and a fixed bag can't score it. Exploration needs closed-loop runs in simulation, with replay kept for estimation-only tracks.

Overhead 'watchtower' webcam as real-world trajectory ground truth: the ground truth must be several times more accurate than the thing it measures. Hinderer's single 1080p ceiling camera at 1.3 m already gives 3–5 cm RMSE, and 45 cm at 3 m with one marker. Autolab reports only repeatability (1.3–3.4 cm SD), not accuracy. So a single webcam ground truth could be about as accurate as B1 and unable to rank estimators near B1. Plan several roof tags, a multi-camera setup, or at least hand-measured waypoint checks, and state the ground-truth error in the benchmark.

The isaac_ros_apriltag point is right in substance, with one addition: Lyrical's Tier 1 Linux platform is Ubuntu 26.04. A Jazzy/Noble Spark would need containers or an OS change, which further supports using apriltag_ros on Jazzy.

esp32-cam-fpv as evidence that HTTP is the bottleneck, and as an optional path: it depends on monitor-mode packet injection to a dedicated receiver. That is incompatible with the normal Wi-Fi network the Pico micro-ROS link uses, so it is not a drop-in fix. The 50–80 ms latency cannot be used as an estimate for HTTP streaming.

The 80–150 ms latency assumption rests on an ESP32-S3 micro-ROS snippet (78 ms median, resolution unknown) and non-HTTP FPV figures. No source measured HTTP/MJPEG latency for an ESP32 with an OV3660. The stop-and-look protocol is still sensible, but the numbers are a guess.

Data association 'trivial for both classical and LLM estimators': true only when the LLM is given decoded IDs. The main SLAMDuck failure was systematic range bias, not association. So the benchmark's hard part is metric fusion, which the researcher does acknowledge. The duplicated-ID and hidden-ID conditions are well motivated.
missed: The MathWorks AprilTag landmark-SLAM example uses real data from 'an Axis M1013 network camera at a resolution of 640-by-480' plus Jackal odometry. This is the closest documented pipeline at VGA resolution, and its code is reusable. It reports only optimizer-vs-optimizer differences, not ground-truth error. https://www.mathworks.com/help/nav/ug/landmark-slam-using-apriltag-markers.html

TagSLAM's only demo used tag poses 'deterimined from the wall orientations and from laser distance measurements with a Leica Disto D3a', plus stereo VIO odometry. It is localization/loop closure against a surveyed map, not unknown-map SLAM from wheel odometry. https://arxiv.org/pdf/1910.00679

Abbas et al. 2019 report raw single-tag precision of '112 cm2' (x) and '14 cm2' (y) at 70 cm, i.e. about 10.6 cm standard deviation in x. They also say 'AprilTag's accuracy is maximum when the viewing camera is pointed towards the center of the tag'. https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/b2d4/cd35c7dbfefc50d5192f142504fe2a601f8f.pdf

The apriltag_ros detection message carries 'the original homography matrix, the hamming distance and the decision_margin', but no pose-ambiguity error. The config has pose_estimation_method: "pnp". https://raw.githubusercontent.com/christianrauch/apriltag_ros/master/README.md

The rosdistro release for apriltag_ros on Kilted is 3.2.2-2, not 3.4.0. Humble, Jazzy, Lyrical and Rolling have 3.4.0-1. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ros/rosdistro/master/kilted/distribution.yaml

ROS 2 Lyrical Luth (May 2026) has 'tier 1 support for Windows 11 and Ubuntu 26.04', and REP 2000 no longer covers target platforms from Lyrical on. This matters for isaac_ros_apriltag on the Spark. https://x.com/OpenRoboticsOrg/status/2057860853626437719 (search snippet); https://reps.openrobotics.org/rep-2000/

apriltag-esp32 reports 'No wrong tag detection when using 36h11 family. Sometimes tags might not be detected due to motion blurry or light conditions', and uses about 2.5 MB of memory at SVGA with pose estimation. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raspiduino/apriltag-esp32/master/README.md

esp32-camera README: 'Using YUV or RGB puts a lot of strain on the chip ... image data might be missing. This is particularly true if WiFi is enabled.' Stream JPEG, not raw. https://github.com/espressif/esp32-camera

Hinderer 2025: 'while more markers give lower RMSE, maximum errors can be larger with more markers', and a systematic error from 'imperfect camera calibration' 'does not decrease by adding markers'. Calibration quality sets a floor on the baseline. https://arxiv.org/html/2509.17345

Kalaitzakis et al., 'Fiducial Markers for Pose Estimation: Overview, Applications and Experimental Comparison of the ARTag, AprilTag, ArUco and STag Markers', J. Intell. Robot. Syst. 2021. The snippet reports AprilTag detection rates above 90% on low-resolution Logitech and piCam data. Accuracy tables were not retrieved. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10846-020-01307-9

SPM-SLAM (Muñoz-Salinas, Marín-Jiménez, Medina-Carnicer, Pattern Recognition 86:156-171, 2019) is marker-only SLAM from squared planar markers. It is a closer classical baseline than UcoSLAM for a tag-only arena. Accuracy numbers were not retrieved. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0031320318303224

The Duckietown Autolab gives repeatability, not accuracy: 'standard deviation for the MPD of 3.4 cm' (and 1.3 cm, 2.5 cm in other settings). This bounds how good a watchtower-style ground truth can be shown to be. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.04362

In AprilTag 2's real-image test, 'The camera was aligned with the center tag of the mosaic, and moved perpendicularly away from the mosaic plane', with laser-tape ground truth and rectified images. The accuracy plots are for a frontal geometry. https://april.eecs.umich.edu/pdfs/wang2016iros.pdf

FMAC (Laurent & Sandoz, arXiv:2601.07723, Jan 2026) is a physically based synthetic renderer for fair fiducial pose-accuracy comparison. It could generate ESP32-CAM-like degraded images for a simulated accuracy study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07723

research.summary: All four frontier models the student named exist and can be called as tool-using, image-reading agents as of 2026-09-27. They are all reasoning models, though, and that shapes how the benchmark has to work. OpenAI's API docs list GPT-6 Astra (`gpt-6-astra`, released Sep 3, 2026, $10/$50 per MTok) and GPT-6 Sol (`gpt-6-sol`, released Sep 22, 2026, $2/$10). There is also a cheaper third tier, GPT-6 Luna (`gpt-6-luna`, $0.10/$0.50). All three accept text and image input, support function calling, and have a 1.05M-token context window with 128K max output. Astra has no `none` reasoning effort, so its lowest setting is `low`. Anthropic's docs list Claude Opus 5.5 (`claude-opus-5-5`, released Sep 22, 2026, $4/$20) and Claude Fable 5.1 (`claude-fable-5-1`, released Sep 1, 2026, $10/$50). Both take text and images, use tools, have 1M context and 128K output, and have thinking always on. Both reject forced `tool_choice` (`any`/`tool`) and non-default sampling settings; the no-custom-temperature rule is verified for Fable 5.1, and for Astra it comes from a paraphrase. Artificial Analysis measures time-to-first-token (TTFT, the wait before any output appears) of about 6 s for Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 at low effort. It measures about 36 s for Sol at xhigh and about 98 s for Astra at xhigh, and minutes at max effort. On the local side, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B are Apache-2.0 native vision-language models. Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it supports images and native function calling with a `gemma4` vLLM tool parser. Published DGX Spark decode speeds are roughly 21–30 tok/s for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 on vLLM, about 24.5 tok/s for Qwen3.8-27B on vLLM (34–38 on SGLang with speculative decoding), and about 52 tok/s for Gemma 4 26B-A4B NVFP4. Dense 31B Gemma runs at about 7 tok/s. NVIDIA's official Spark figures are 128 GB unified memory and 273 GB/s bandwidth. GLM-5.3-Flash (320B total) and Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B are open-weight but too large for one Spark. I could not verify a 2026 Llama or a current general-purpose InternVL release from official sources.

implications: INFERENCE: The student's model names are right, with small fixes. The API IDs are gpt-6-astra, gpt-6-sol, claude-opus-5-5 and claude-fable-5-1. GPT-6 Luna ($0.10/$0.50) is a cheap, low-latency OpenAI tier worth adding as a baseline. Claude Sonnet 5 and Haiku 4.5 play the same role on the Anthropic side.

INFERENCE: Latency rules out continuous closed-loop control by any frontier model. Measured TTFT runs from about 6 s at low effort (Opus 5.5 / Fable 5.1) to minutes at max effort, and Astra has no 'none' effort. The design must be stop-perceive-think-act: the robot halts, the model returns one bounded move, and the Pico runs it. This matches the rule that the LLM stays out of the motor loop. The benchmark should fix the effort level per model and report wall-clock per decision and per episode alongside accuracy.

INFERENCE: Sampling can't be made deterministic. Fable 5.1 rejects non-default temperature/top_p/top_k, and Astra reportedly disallows custom temperature/top_p. So temperature=0 is not an option: run N≥3–5 trials per condition and report mean and variance.

INFERENCE: The harness needs a provider abstraction. Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 reject forced tool_choice, so use tool_choice auto plus strict: true schemas and count a turn with no tool call as a logged failure or retry. Astra reportedly requires the Responses API for tool calls. Local models run through vLLM's OpenAI-compatible endpoint with the qwen3_coder or gemma4 tool parsers.

INFERENCE: Preserved thinking on Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 conflicts with the natural 'LLM as SLAM' design of rewriting a map summary in the system prompt every step. For accounts created after Aug 31, 2026 that returns 400 errors. There are two options. The first is stateless per-step calls: a fresh conversation each step, with the serialized beacon map, pose belief and new observation as the only input. This is also the fairest way to compare models. The second is strictly append-only conversations with state updates delivered as new messages.

INFERENCE: Anthropic's docs describe Claude's coordinate and localization outputs as approximate. So the benchmark should separate two roles. (a) A classical AprilTag detector front-end (tag ID, range, bearing from the known tag size and camera intrinsics) feeding the LLM, which does the estimation, data association and loop closure. (b) A raw-image VLM variant, run as an ablation. Without that split, a model's failure to measure pixels can't be told apart from a failure at SLAM reasoning.

INFERENCE: Image input is cheap. A 640×480 ESP32-CAM frame is ceil(640/28)×ceil(480/28) = 23×18 = 414 Claude visual tokens, about $0.0017 per frame on Opus 5.5. Output reasoning tokens will dominate cost. As a rough example, 200 steps × (5k in + 2k out) comes to about $30 per run on Fable 5.1 or Astra, about $12 on Opus 5.5, about $6 on Sol and about $0.20 on Luna, before caching or batching.

INFERENCE: For local models, decode speed of about 20–50 tok/s on the Spark means a 1–2k-token thinking trace costs 40–100 s per step. Run local models with thinking off or at low reasoning effort, cap output tokens, and prefer MoE models (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B) over dense ones. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B supersedes the cached Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at the same size, with better vendor-reported RefCOCO and EmbSpatial scores. It is worth adding.

INFERENCE: Some models don't fit a single 128 GB Spark: GLM-5.3-Flash at 320B total (roughly 160 GB or more even at 4 bits) and Qwen3.8-2.4T. Reasonable local candidates are Qwen3.5/3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.8-27B (FP8 or NVFP4), Gemma-4-26B-A4B, GLM-4.6V-Flash 9B (it has native grounding), possibly Llama 4 Scout at Int4 (2025 vintage), and gpt-oss-120b as a text-only 'SLAM back-end' baseline fed detector output.

INFERENCE: Handling safety refusals and fallbacks matters for the benchmark. Anthropic's server-side fallbacks retry refused requests on a different model, which would silently contaminate per-model results. Either disable fallbacks in benchmark runs or log the model that actually answered and the stop_reason on every call.

implication_challenges: LATENCY (partly wrong): 'measured TTFT runs from about 6 s at low effort' is only true for the Claude models and the asymmetric AA pairings picked. Artificial Analysis reports GPT-6 Sol (Non-reasoning) at 1.10 s TTFT (https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/releases/gpt-6-sol) and GPT-6 Luna (low) at 2.16 s TTFT (https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/gpt-6-luna-low). The frontier floor is therefore about 1–2 s, not 6 s. Only Astra (minimum 'low'), Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 (thinking always on) cannot go to zero reasoning. Stop-perceive-think-act is still the right design, but comparing Claude at low with GPT at xhigh/max makes OpenAI look much slower than it has to be. The benchmark should compare at matched effort tiers. AA's TTFT includes thinking time on AA's own text prompts, not image+tool prompts, so it is only a loose proxy.

DETERMINISM (overstated): 'temperature=0 is not an option' holds for Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Astra. OpenAI's GPT-6 guide says only 'When reasoning effort is not `none`, remove `temperature`, `top_p`...' (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latest-model.md), so Sol and Luna at effort none, and all local vLLM/Ollama models, do accept temperature. Temperature is thus a confound between providers, not something none of them allow. Repeated trials (N>=3–5) are still correct, because temperature 0 was never deterministic anyway.

HARNESS (incomplete): the Responses-API requirement is not Astra-only. Sol and Luna 'support function calling in Chat Completions only with `reasoning_effort: "none"`. Use Responses for reasoning with tools.' (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-sol.md). Any OpenAI tool-calling run with reasoning on must go through Responses. Qwen3.8-27B uses the `qwen3_xml` parser, not qwen3_coder (https://recipes.vllm.ai/Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B).

PRESERVED THINKING (partly overstated): 'rewriting a map summary in the system prompt every step ... returns 400 errors' only applies if you replay earlier thinking blocks inside the same conversation. The fully stateless per-step design avoids it completely. Anthropic also documents an append-only route: mid-conversation system messages, plus turn-scoped system messages (`clear_at: "next_user_message"`) on Fable 5.1, or `prefix_mismatch_behavior: "drop_block"`. The researcher's two options are fine but not the only ones.

FALLBACK CONTAMINATION (overstated): server-side fallback is opt-in. You must set `fallbacks` ("default" or a list) and send the `server-side-fallback-2026-07-01` beta header. The response 'names the model that served it' through the top-level `model` field and a `fallback_message` entry in usage.iterations (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/refusals-and-fallback). It is not silent unless the student turns it on and never logs `model`. Logging `model` and `stop_reason` is still good practice. Artificial Analysis's own Opus 5.5 numbers carry a 'Default Fallback' label, so third-party latency figures may themselves be fallback-mixed.

COST ARITHMETIC (small error): at $0.10/$0.50, Luna comes to 200×(5000×0.1+2000×0.5)/1e6 = $0.30, not $0.20. The Fable 5.1 and Astra ($30), Opus ($12) and Sol ($6) figures check out. The Claude image token count (23×18 = 414 tokens, about $0.0017 on Opus 5.5) is correct. OpenAI's image cost for Astra is different: 32-px patches × 1.2 multiplier, so 640×480 is 20×15 = 300 patches, about 360 tokens (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/images-vision.md).

LOCAL LATENCY (minor): '1–2k-token thinking trace costs 40–100 s' at 20–50 tok/s is actually 20–100 s. Qwen3.8-27B thinks at xhigh by default, so enable_thinking must be set to false explicitly. The Gemma 31B '7 tok/s' figure is BF16, not NVFP4, so 'prefer MoE' is right but overstated for a quantized dense model.

MODEL FIT (unverified leap): 'GLM-5.3-Flash does not fit a single Spark' is right at 4 bits (about 160 GB), but the card lists 122 community quantizations. A roughly 2–3-bit GGUF might fit in 128 GB. Mark it 'unverified; likely impractical' rather than impossible.

CANDIDATE LIST (stale): 'possibly Llama 4 Scout at Int4 (2025 vintage)' ignores Meta's Aug 2026 open-weight VLM Muse Glimmer 30B, which is vLLM-verified on DGX Spark, as the stronger Meta candidate. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is not Spark-verified in vLLM recipes; Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B are.

ANTHROPIC-SIDE BASELINES: calling Sonnet 5 and Haiku 4.5 cheaper baselines is supported ($2/$10 'Fast'; $1/$5 'Fastest'). Sonnet 5's thinking is 'Adaptive' but not listed as always-on, and Haiku 4.5 uses extended (manual) thinking, so both can likely run without thinking. Of the four Claude models, those two are the only ones where a low-latency no-thinking run is plausible. That is an inference from the models table and was not directly tested.

research.summary: The manipulation VLAs with open weights (OpenVLA 7B, pi0/pi0-FAST/pi0.5 through openpi, SmolVLA 450M, NVIDIA GR00T N1.x at 3B, Octo 27M/93M) map camera images and a language instruction straight to low-level action chunks for arms or humanoids. RT-2/RT-2-X are described as closed. No source claims any of these works on a new embodiment without fine-tuning: OpenVLA says it "only works well on domains from the training dataset", openpi says pi0 "may or may not work for you", and GR00T supports zero-shot only on its pretraining embodiments. The only one that drives a base is pi0.5, which commands base velocities for a holonomic mobile manipulator, and its authors list multi-room navigation as future work. Navigation foundation models are a closer fit. GNM, ViNT and NoMaD are 19-31M-parameter RGB policies that output normalized waypoints, and NoMaD adds goal-free exploration. CrossFormer and OmniVLA are cross-embodiment or omni-goal VLAs. X-Mobility sends velocity commands to a differential-drive Nova Carter with zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. NaVILA, NaVid, Uni-NaVid, NavFoM and InternVLA-N1 are 7-8B video-VLM navigators that output language moves such as "moving forward 75cm", discrete FORWARD 25 cm / TURN 30° actions, or trajectories. None of these sources describes a model that estimates metric pose or builds a landmark map. ViNT's own robots use wheel odometry or GPS "to track their position", OmniVLA takes a GPS pose, X-Mobility's ROS 2 demo needs a map and a clicked 2D Goal Pose, GemNav gets its pose from LiDAR-inertial SLAM, and NaVid simply works "without any maps, odometers, or depth inputs". The one mapping-like ability is topological: GNM, ViNT and NoMaD keep a graph of past camera images as nodes and localize by finding "the node with smallest temporal distance". This is appearance-based place recognition, a fair baseline for the revisit (loop-closure) sub-task but not for metric SLAM. There is evidence of running on aarch64: GR00T N1.7 officially supports DGX Spark (CUDA 13.0), a community project ran pi0.5 on a DGX Spark at about 95 ms with TensorRT FP8+NVFP4, a GR00T N1.5 fine-tuning guide for Spark lists aarch64 workarounds, NVIDIA has a pi0.5 tutorial for Jetson Thor, OpenVLA INT4 runs on a Jetson AGX Orin at about 375 ms, and NoMaD/ViNT were deployed on Jetson Orin. Overall, putting VLAs or navigation models on a SLAM leaderboard would compare unlike things. They should enter the benchmark through a shared bounded-move action interface, as exploration or navigation policies and as place-recognition baselines, and be reported as N/A on pose and map accuracy.

claims.claim: OpenVLA (Moo Jin Kim et al., 2024, arXiv:2406.09246, 'OpenVLA: An Open-Source Vision-Language-Action Model') is a 7B open-weight VLA trained on 970k real robot demonstrations for manipulation; it describes RT-2-X as a closed model.
claims.quote: outperforming closed models such as RT-2-X (55B) by 16.5% in absolute task success rate across 29 tasks and multiple robot embodiments, with 7x fewer parameters

claims.claim: OpenVLA outputs 7-DoF end-effector actions that must be un-normalized per dataset (e.g. unnorm_key='bridge_orig'), and the repo states it does not transfer to new domains or embodiments without fine-tuning.
claims.quote: Out-of-the-box, it only works well on domains from the training dataset.

claims.claim: RT-2 (Anthony Brohan et al., 2023, arXiv:2307.15818) represents robot actions as text tokens inside a VLM. The RT-2 abstract page does not say whether weights were released; OpenVLA calls RT-2-X 'closed'.
claims.quote: we express the actions as text tokens and incorporate them directly into the training set of the model in the same way as natural language tokens

claims.claim: pi0 (Kevin Black et al., 2024, arXiv:2410.24164, 'π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control') is a flow-matching VLA trained on single-arm, dual-arm and mobile-manipulator data.
claims.quote: a large and diverse dataset from multiple dexterous robot platforms, including single-arm robots, dual-arm robots, and mobile manipulators

claims.claim: pi0.5 (Physical Intelligence, 2025, arXiv:2504.16054) runs on mobile manipulators with a wheeled holonomic base and outputs base velocities at 50 Hz, but the authors name navigating between rooms as future work.
claims.quote: directly commands target poses for the arms, gripper, and torso lift, and the target base velocities at 50 Hz

claims.claim: openpi releases pi0, pi0-FAST and pi0.5 base checkpoints plus fine-tuned DROID, ALOHA and LIBERO checkpoints (no mobile-robot checkpoint). It warns that transfer to other robots is not guaranteed, needs more than 8 GB of GPU memory for inference, and has only been tested on Ubuntu 22.04.
claims.quote: The repo has been tested with Ubuntu 22.04, we do not currently support other operating systems.

claims.claim: SmolVLA (Mustafa Shukor et al., 2025, arXiv:2506.01844) is a roughly 450M-parameter VLA trained on community SO-100/SO-101 arm datasets. It outputs flow-matching action chunks and is meant for consumer GPUs or CPUs.
claims.quote: designed to be trained on a single GPU and deployed on consumer-grade GPUs or even CPUs

claims.claim: The SmolVLA base checkpoint is intended to be fine-tuned for each robot or use case.
claims.quote: Base model to fine tune on your specific use case

claims.claim: GR00T N1 (Johan Bjorck et al., 2025, arXiv:2503.14734) is an open humanoid VLA with a VLM 'System 2' and a diffusion-transformer 'System 1' that generates motor actions.
claims.quote: The subsequent diffusion transformer module (System 1) generates fluid motor actions in real time.

claims.claim: The Isaac-GR00T repo's latest model is GR00T N1.7-3B. It officially supports DGX Spark (CUDA 13.0) and Jetson Thor/Orin, but zero-shot only on pretraining embodiments (manipulation tags plus Unitree G1 whole-body); new embodiments need fine-tuning. Nothing mentions navigation.
claims.quote: DGX Spark on CUDA 13.0 with Python 3.12

claims.claim: Octo (Octo Model Team, 2024, arXiv:2405.12213) is trained on 800k Open X-Embodiment manipulation trajectories and can be fine-tuned to new observation and action spaces. The repo lists Octo-Small (27M) and Octo-Base (93M), which predict 4-step action chunks.
claims.quote: 800k trajectories from the Open X-Embodiment dataset, the largest robot manipulation dataset to date

claims.claim: CrossFormer (Ria Doshi et al., 2024, arXiv:2408.11812) is a 130M open cross-embodiment policy covering manipulation, wheeled navigation, quadrupeds and drones. For navigation it outputs 2D relative waypoints, and at deployment it needs a topological map built by teleoperating the robot first.
claims.quote: We first obtain a topological map of the environment by teleoperating the robot. Then, at every time-step we find the closest node in the map

claims.claim: GNM (Dhruv Shah et al., 2022, arXiv:2210.03370, 'GNM: A General Navigation Model to Drive Any Robot') is trained on 60 hours of navigation data from 6 robots. It predicts normalized waypoints plus a temporal distance, and it localizes topologically by matching the current camera image to the nearest image node in a graph.
claims.quote: At every time step, the robot associates its current and goal observations in M, i.e., finds the node with smallest temporal distance to it, and computes the optimal sequence of subgoals

claims.claim: GNM's action space is relative waypoints plus yaw, scaled by each robot's top speed; a robot-specific controller then turns the waypoints into velocities.
claims.quote: a robot-specific controller can be used to (i) unnormalize the waypoints, and (ii) track them (e.g., PID, MPPI) to extract low-level commands

claims.claim: ViNT (Dhruv Shah et al., 2023, arXiv:2306.14846) is a 31M-parameter model that runs at 4 Hz, outputs relative waypoints, and builds a topological graph on the fly while exploring. It uses external odometry or GPS for position rather than estimating pose itself.
claims.quote: The robots have access to onboard wheel odometry (indoors), GPS coordinates (outdoors), or passive satellite imagery (outdoors), to track their position.

claims.claim: NoMaD (Ajay Sridhar et al., 2023, arXiv:2310.07896) is a 19M-parameter goal-masked diffusion policy that handles both goal-free exploration and goal-reaching. It keeps an episodic graph of past image observations, uses frontier-based exploration, and runs on a Jetson Orin.
claims.quote: a graph structure with nodes corresponding to the robot's visual observations in the environment, and edges corresponding to navigable paths between two nodes

claims.claim: The official visualnav-transformer release (ROS Noetic, LoCoBot with a Jetson Orin Nano) builds its topomaps from a teleoperated rosbag, and its exploration script only lets NoMaD wander at random. It recommends a wide-angle (fisheye) RGB camera.
claims.quote: script that deploys a trained NoMaD model on the robot to randomly explore its environment

claims.claim: The visualnav-transformer README claims zero-shot control of many robots and lists a wide-angle camera as the recommended sensor.
claims.quote: A wide-angle RGB camera: [Example](...ELP-170degree-Fisheye...)

claims.claim: A community ROS 2 port of GNM/ViNT/NoMaD supports ROS 2 Jazzy and Humble with Docker images for CUDA, ROCm or CPU, and publishes waypoints plus cmd_vel.
claims.quote: ROS2 Jazzy (Ubuntu 24.04) and Humble (Ubuntu 22.04)

claims.claim: NaVILA (An-Chieh Cheng et al., 2024, arXiv:2412.04453) is a two-level VLA whose VLM outputs mid-level moves as language, which a locomotion RL policy then executes. The 8B weights (a8cheng/navila-llama3-8b-8f) are released.
claims.quote: mid-level actions with spatial information in the form of language, (e.g., 'moving forward 75cm')

claims.claim: NaVid (Jiazhao Zhang et al., 2024, arXiv:2402.15852) is a video-VLM navigator that uses a monocular RGB stream only and explicitly no map or odometry.
claims.quote: without any maps, odometers, or depth inputs

claims.claim: Uni-NaVid (Jiazhao Zhang et al., 2024, arXiv:2412.06224) outputs discrete bounded moves, FORWARD 25 cm and TURN 30°, predicting four at a time. It ran at about 5 Hz on a remote A100 server. The 7B (Vicuna-7B) weights are released.
claims.quote: {FORWARD, TURN-LEFT, TURN-RIGHT, STOP}

claims.claim: NavFoM (Jiazhao Zhang et al., 2025, arXiv:2509.12129, 'Embodied Navigation Foundation Model') is trained on 8M samples across quadrupeds, drones, wheeled robots and vehicles. It predicts a trajectory for each robot's own local planner and ran on a remote RTX 5090. The project page links no weights.
claims.quote: is subsequently processed by the local planner of each individual robot, which sends appropriate commands

claims.claim: OmniVLA (Noriaki Hirose, Catherine Glossop, Dhruv Shah, Sergey Levine, 2025, arXiv:2509.19480) is an OpenVLA-based navigation VLA that takes goals as 2D poses, images or language. Checkpoints, including omnivla-edge, are on Hugging Face. Its inference takes a GPS pose as input.
claims.quote: 2D poses, egocentric images, and natural language, as well as their combinations

claims.claim: X-Mobility (Wei Liu et al., 2024, arXiv:2410.17491) is an NVIDIA navigation model trained in Isaac Sim that outputs linear and angular velocities. It was deployed zero-shot on a differential-drive Nova Carter.
claims.quote: We successfully deployed X-Mobility on a Nova Carter robot without any fine-tuning, demonstrating its real-time navigation capabilities through zero-shot Sim2Real transfer.

claims.claim: X-Mobility's ROS 2 demo uses Isaac Sim 4.2 with Carter and Nav2. The goal is a pose clicked on a known map, so the model consumes localization rather than producing it. Its model card says its route input is given 'from robot position' and it runs via TensorRT on Jetson Orin.
claims.quote: Select `2D Goal Pose` and then click on the map to set a position / orientation.

claims.claim: InternNav / InternVLA-N1 is a Qwen2.5-VL-based dual-system navigation model with open weights. Its DualVLN variant needs RGB only, but its NavDP variant needs RGB-D (depth).
claims.quote: RGB-D

claims.claim: GemNav (Peter Böhm et al., 2026, arXiv:2607.06882) fine-tunes Gemma-4 E2B to output waypoint tokens. It does no mapping or exploration and takes its pose from an external LiDAR-inertial SLAM system.
claims.quote: body-frame pose recovered online from a continuous-time 3D LiDAR-inertial SLAM system

claims.claim: Mobility VLA (Hao-Tien Lewis Chiang et al., 2024, arXiv:2407.07775) pairs a long-context VLM that picks the goal frame from a pre-recorded tour video with a topological graph built offline; it is not an unknown-environment system.
claims.quote: A low-level policy uses the goal frame and an offline constructed topological graph to generate robot actions.

claims.claim: A 2026 VLN survey with real-robot tests (Liuyi Wang et al., arXiv:2607.09792) found a large sim-to-real drop for monolithic RGB-only navigation models, while hierarchical systems held up better.
claims.quote: a representative monolithic RGB-only method achieves 61% success in simulation but drops to 22% in real-world deployment

claims.claim: EmbodiedBench (Rui Yang et al., 2025, arXiv:2502.09560) tested 24 multimodal LLMs on high-level and low-level embodied tasks: they do well at the high level and poorly at low-level atomic actions.
claims.quote: MLLMs excel at high-level tasks but struggle with low-level manipulation, with the best model, GPT-4o, scoring only 28.9% on average

claims.claim: On a Jetson AGX Orin, OpenVLA takes about 955 ms per inference at BF16 (15.2 GB) and about 375 ms at INT4 (4.0 GB) (Seongmin Park et al., 2024, arXiv:2412.01034).
claims.quote: the INT4 model achieves a 2.5× speedup compared to BFloat16

claims.claim: A community DGX Spark project (GB10, aarch64, CUDA 13) ran openpi pi0.5 inference at about 203 ms in PyTorch BF16 and about 94.7 ms with TensorRT FP8+NVFP4.
claims.quote: openpi pi0.5 vision-language-action inference at 94.7 ms on TensorRT FP8 and NVFP4, 2.12x PyTorch BF16 at cosine 0.997

claims.claim: NVIDIA's Jetson AI Lab has an official pi0.5 (openpi) tutorial for Jetson AGX Thor using aarch64 wheels, reporting about 49 ms latency with TensorRT FP8+NVFP4.
claims.quote: TensorRT FP8 + NVFP4: ~49 ms

claims.claim: A GitHub guide (Dec 2025) got GR00T N1.5 fine-tuning working on DGX Spark (sm_121, CUDA 13.0, aarch64) only after working around the pinned PyTorch version, flash-attention, PyTorch3D and decord.
claims.quote: the `pyproject.toml` specifies `torch==2.5.1` which doesn't support CUDA 13.0 or the sm_121 compute capability

claims.claim: VLM-GLoc (Shivendra Agrawal et al., 2026, arXiv:2605.30506) uses a VLM as the semantic observation front-end inside Monte Carlo Localization, keeping the classical estimator rather than replacing it.
claims.quote: a unified semantic observation front-end

implications: INFERENCE: Manipulation VLAs (OpenVLA, pi0/pi0.5, SmolVLA, GR00T N1.x, Octo) do not belong on a SLAM leaderboard. None estimates pose or a landmark map, and none has been shown to drive an unseen differential-drive car without teleop data and fine-tuning. Either leave them out, or add one (pi0.5 or SmolVLA via LeRobot) as an optional 'fine-tuned end-to-end explorer', stating clearly that it was fine-tuned on this car and needs the geometry from a separate estimator.

INFERENCE: Navigation foundation models enter at two points. (a) As the exploration/navigation policy that picks the next move. (b) As appearance-based place-recognition baselines for revisit detection: GNM/ViNT/NoMaD's temporal-distance head finds 'the node with smallest temporal distance'. They should get 'N/A' on metric pose error and landmark-map error, because in every source they consume odometry, GPS, or a prior map and do not produce one.

INFERENCE / design suggestion: make the benchmark capability-decomposed, with a shared I/O contract. T1 (estimation): replay identical logged episodes (JPEG frames, encoder odometry, IMU yaw, AprilTag detections) to every LLM/VLM agent and to a classical landmark-SLAM reference; score robot pose and tag-map error. T2 (loop closure): given a frame plus history, is this a revisit? Compare LLM/VLM against the NoMaD/ViNT distance head and a tag-ID oracle. T3 (exploration policy): every model chooses among the same bounded moves, localized by a common classical back end so only the policy differs; score tags found per metre, coverage, collisions and path length. T4 (full LLM-as-SLAM closed loop): LLM/VLM agents only, plus a hybrid where NoMaD explores and the LLM maps.

INFERENCE: The student's bounded high-level move API lines up with published navigation outputs: Uni-NaVid's FORWARD 25 cm / TURN 30°, NaVILA's 'moving forward 75cm', and GNM/ViNT/NoMaD waypoints that a PD controller already converts to velocities. Adapters can therefore quantize waypoints or trajectories into the same move set the LLM uses. That keeps every model out of the motor loop and makes the comparison fair.

INFERENCE: Run the robot stop-and-go: it waits for each decision, then executes a bounded move. Report wall-clock latency separately. This stops API-model latency from confounding accuracy, and allows exact replay in simulation. The latencies found span roughly 50 ms to 1 s: pi0.5 about 95 ms on a Spark, OpenVLA INT4 about 375 ms on Orin, ViNT at 4 Hz, Uni-NaVid about 5 Hz on an A100.

INFERENCE / risk: GNM/ViNT/NoMaD were trained on and recommend a wide-angle fisheye camera, while the ESP32-CAM OV3660 is a low-mounted, probably narrower camera sending JPEG over Wi-Fi. Zero-shot navigation performance will likely drop. Fit a wide-angle lens, or record in Isaac Sim/Gazebo a camera model that matches the real one, and treat the real-world numbers as a sim-to-real stress test (the VLN survey found 61% to 22% for monolithic RGB-only models).

INFERENCE: Models that need depth (InternVLA-N1's NavDP variant) or LiDAR/GPS pose (GemNav, OmniVLA's pose goals, X-Mobility's map-based goals) do not fit the fixed hardware, which has no range sensor and no localization in an unknown map. Good real-robot candidates are RGB-only NoMaD/ViNT/GNM (small, easy on the Spark), and possibly Uni-NaVid or NaVILA (7-8B, fit in 121 GB unified memory).

INFERENCE: On the DGX Spark, GR00T N1.7 has official support and pi0.5 has community proof of running, but openpi officially supports only Ubuntu 22.04, and GR00T N1.5 on Spark needed hand-built aarch64 dependencies. Plan time for dependency workarounds, and prefer the small PyTorch navigation models (NoMaD/ViNT) as the first navigation-model baseline.

INFERENCE: X-Mobility already has an Isaac Sim + Carter + ROS 2 pipeline and outputs velocities for a differential drive, so it is a natural simulation-only navigation baseline, provided the classical localization back end supplies its route/goal. It cannot serve in an unknown-map localization track.

INFERENCE: The literature (VLM-GLoc, GemNav, ViNT) consistently uses VLMs, VLAs and navigation models around a classical pose estimator, not in place of one. So the 'LLM as SLAM' claim should be tested against a hybrid ablation (LLM front-end, classical EKF or factor-graph back end) as well as the classical reference, and the writeup should say the pure-LLM estimator is the novel, unproven part.
unknowns: The ESP32-CAM OV3660 module's field of view and lens options, and whether GNM/ViNT/NoMaD work zero-shot with a narrow, low-mounted, Wi-Fi JPEG camera on a small TT-motor car; no source found.

No direct evidence found that GNM/ViNT/NoMaD, NaVILA, Uni-NaVid, NavFoM or InternVLA-N1 have run on aarch64 or a DGX Spark. NoMaD/ViNT evidence covers Jetson Orin only; the 7-8B navigation VLMs were run on x86 A100 or RTX 5090 servers.
Whether the released NoMaD code can build a topological graph online during frontier exploration: the paper describes it, but the released explore script only explores randomly.
Whether NavFoM weights are publicly released; the project page links no code or weights.
OmniVLA-edge parameter count and inference compute; exact inference memory for NaVILA-8B and Uni-NaVid-7B.
RT-2 weight status confirmed from a primary Google/DeepMind source; only OpenVLA's description of RT-2-X as 'closed' was seen.

Whether any VLA has been fine-tuned or evaluated on a small differential-drive toy car. Community SmolVLA checkpoints exist for the holonomic LeKiwi base, but their base action format was not confirmed.

Any published benchmark that evaluates VLAs or navigation models on metric localization or landmark-map accuracy (ATE, map error); none found, which suggests there is no standard way to score them on this.
The model names 'GPT 6 Astra', 'GPT 6 Sol' and 'Fable 5.1' were outside this topic and were not verified here.
The formal definitions of navigation metrics (SPL etc.) were not fetched: the Anderson et al. 2018 (arXiv:1807.06757) abstract page did not include them.

verdicts.claim: OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024, arXiv:2406.09246) is a 7B open-weight VLA trained on 970k real robot demonstrations; describes RT-2-X as closed.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim in the v3 abstract ('outperforming closed models such as RT-2-X (55B) by 16.5%...'), and the abstract also contains '970k'. First author: Moo Jin Kim, 2024/06/13.

verdicts.claim: OpenVLA outputs 7-DoF actions un-normalized per dataset (unnorm_key='bridge_orig'); repo says it does not transfer without fine-tuning.
verdicts.note: README: '# Predict Action (7-DoF; un-normalize for BridgeData V2)' and 'unnorm_key="bridge_orig"'. The quote is verbatim. The full sentence is stronger: 'OpenVLA typically requires fine-tuning on a small demonstration dataset (~100 demos) from your target domain robot. Out-of-the-box, it only works well on domains from the training dataset.'

verdicts.claim: RT-2 (Brohan et al., 2023, arXiv:2307.15818) expresses actions as text tokens; weights status not stated on abstract; OpenVLA calls RT-2-X closed.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim in the abstract. OpenVLA's abstract only calls RT-2-X closed, not RT-2. I found no primary Google/DeepMind statement about RT-2 weights; a web-search summary says they were not released, but that is not a primary source.

verdicts.claim: pi0 (Black et al., 2024, arXiv:2410.24164) is a flow-matching VLA trained on single-arm, dual-arm and mobile-manipulator data.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim in the abstract. Note that 'mobile manipulators' here means manipulation platforms, not navigation robots.

verdicts.claim: pi0.5 (arXiv:2504.16054) runs on holonomic-base mobile manipulators, commands base velocities at 50 Hz; authors list navigating between rooms as future work.
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'directly commands target poses for the arms, gripper, and torso lift, and the target base velocities at 50 Hz (with action chunking)'. The base is 'a wheeled holonomic base' and its action space is 2D linear plus 1D angular velocity. Future work: 'tasks that require navigating between different rooms or remembering where objects are stored'. The released openpi pi0.5 checkpoints are for LIBERO and DROID only, so no base-velocity checkpoint is public.

verdicts.claim: openpi releases pi0/pi0-FAST/pi0.5 base + DROID/ALOHA/LIBERO checkpoints (no mobile); warns transfer not guaranteed; >8 GB inference; tested only Ubuntu 22.04.
verdicts.note: All parts are verified in the README: the checkpoint table (pi0_base, pi0_fast_base, pi05_base, *_droid, *_aloha_*, pi05_libero), 'Inference > 8 GB', 'The repo has been tested with Ubuntu 22.04, we do not currently support other operating systems', and 'pi0 may or may not work for you'. The README also says 'we currently only support the flow matching head' for pi0.5.

verdicts.claim: SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025, arXiv:2506.01844) ~450M, trained on community SO-100/SO-101 datasets, flow-matching chunks, consumer GPUs/CPUs.
verdicts.note: The abstract quote is verbatim. The HTML says 'Our main model, contains 450 million parameters, with approximately 100 million dedicated to the action expert'. The real-world evaluation uses SO-100 and SO-101 arms, and the abstract stresses 'community-collected data'. All of it is manipulation.

verdicts.claim: SmolVLA base checkpoint intended to be fine-tuned per robot/use case.
verdicts.note: The model card states 'Base model to fine tune on your specific use case' and lists 0.5B params. The card does not mention a mobile base or LeKiwi.

verdicts.claim: GR00T N1 (Bjorck et al., 2025, arXiv:2503.14734) is an open humanoid VLA with VLM System 2 and diffusion-transformer System 1.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim. Citation detail: arXiv lists the first author as 'NVIDIA', followed by Johan Bjorck, so 'NVIDIA et al.' or 'Bjorck et al.' both appear in citations.

verdicts.claim: Isaac-GR00T latest is N1.7-3B; officially supports DGX Spark (CUDA 13.0) and Jetson Thor/Orin; zero-shot only on pretraining embodiments (manipulation tags plus Unitree G1 whole-body); nothing on navigation.
verdicts.note: Confirmed: 'nvidia/GR00T-N1.7-3B', 'DGX Spark on CUDA 13.0 with Python 3.12', Thor/Orin on JetPack 7.2 / CUDA 13.2, 'zero-shot inference on pretrain embodiments, or finetune for new tasks', and no mention of navigation. The G1 tag is relative end-effector plus joint, not whole-body. UNITREE_G1_SONIC is a posttrain tag. The README also says inference needs '16 GB+ VRAM' and a gated Cosmos-Reason2-2B backbone.

verdicts.claim: Octo (arXiv:2405.12213) trained on 800k OXE manipulation trajectories, fine-tunable to new obs/action spaces; Octo-Small 27M / Octo-Base 93M, 4-step chunks.
verdicts.note: The abstract quote is verbatim. The repo lists Octo-Base (93M) and Octo-Small (27M) and says it was 'pretrained with an action chunking size of 4'.

verdicts.claim: CrossFormer (Doshi et al., 2024, arXiv:2408.11812) 130M cross-embodiment incl. wheeled nav; outputs 2D relative waypoints; deployment needs a teleop-built topological map.
verdicts.note: Verified: 'our model has 130M parameters' and 'Navigation waypoints: A 2-dimensional action denoting a waypoint relative to the robot's current position... at 4Hz'. The quote is verbatim apart from the math symbol M. It also says it combines the policy 'with the graph-based planner and distance function from Shah et al.', so localization within the graph comes from GNM's distance head, not from CrossFormer.

verdicts.claim: GNM (Shah et al., 2022, arXiv:2210.03370): 60h from 6 robots; predicts normalized waypoints + temporal distance; localizes topologically by nearest image node.
verdicts.note: The abstract has '60 hours of navigation trajectories from 6 distinct robots', and the HTML quote is verbatim ('finds the node with smallest temporal distance to it... using Dijkstra's algorithm'). The graph is built from a prior traversal. This is topological association, not metric localization.

verdicts.claim: GNM action space is relative waypoints + yaw scaled by top speed; robot-specific controller converts to velocities.
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'a robot-specific controller can be used to (i) unnormalize the waypoints, and (ii) track them (e.g., PID, MPPI)'. Also 'relative waypoints p(x,y) and yaw change ψ' and 'scaled by a robot-specific factor α corresponding to the top speed'.

implication_challenges: Tag-ID loop closure is trivial. AprilTag 36h11 IDs are unique, so a 'tag-ID oracle' solves revisit detection almost perfectly whenever a tag is visible. T2 (loop closure) only discriminates between models if it is scored on tag-free revisits or with deliberately duplicated or aliased tag IDs. Otherwise every model will look good. No source addresses this; it is a design flaw in the proposed T2.

Using the NoMaD/ViNT/GNM temporal-distance head as a loop-closure detector is off-label. The papers use it to associate the current observation with nodes of a graph from a prior or ongoing traversal ('finds the node with smallest temporal distance'). No source evaluates it as a place-recognition detector with precision/recall. Present it as an unvalidated baseline, and add a standard global-descriptor place-recognition baseline; Mobility VLA's hierarchical localizer uses a k-NN global image descriptor.

'N/A on pose and map error' is right for the models as released, but the literature does show hybrids that get metric pose from vision. Mobility VLA localizes by PnP against a COLMAP SfM map (Appendix 7.1). So the classical reference should be stated precisely (e.g. tag-landmark EKF/factor graph with wheel+IMU odometry). 'Consistently uses classical estimators' rests on 3-4 examples (VLM-GLoc, GemNav, ViNT, Mobility VLA). That is suggestive, not a survey-level finding.

Stop-and-go with quantized moves is a distribution shift for GNM/ViNT/NoMaD. They take a fixed-rate temporal context of past frames (ViNT runs at 4 Hz with a PD tracker, receding horizon), and their waypoints are normalized by robot top speed. Quantizing their waypoints into discrete FORWARD/TURN moves and feeding them frames spaced by bounded moves is an untested adapter, so 'fair comparison' is asserted, not shown. By contrast, Uni-NaVid/NaVid were trained on exactly 25 cm / 30° steps ('consistent with all training navigation data'). The shared move set should therefore be 25 cm / 30° so that at least those models run in-distribution.

Recommending Uni-NaVid or NaVILA as 'good real-robot candidates' is a leap. Both are instruction-following VLN models, not exploration or mapping models. NaVILA's mid-level language commands were executed by a legged locomotion RL policy. No source shows either on aarch64 or a DGX Spark. Uni-NaVid's 5 Hz was on an A100, and NaVILA pins an old transformers 4.37.2 stack. Fitting in 121 GB of memory says nothing about whether the model runs or works on this camera.

Applying the VLN survey's 61%->22% drop to NoMaD/ViNT on the ESP32-CAM is an extrapolation. The survey measures monolithic RGB-only VLN models on instruction following, not goal-free exploration policies. The camera-mismatch risk is real (fisheye recommended), but its size is unknown.

Quoting pi0.5 at ~95 ms on Spark and GR00T N1.7 Spark support as benchmark-relevant is misleading. Those latencies are for manipulation checkpoints (pi05_libero / DROID), and no released checkpoint of either model can command a mobile base. Budget time for them only if the student will collect teleop data and fine-tune. Otherwise they should not enter the benchmark at all.

The summary understates LLM/MLLM ability at low-level discrete navigation. EmbodiedBench's 28.9% figure is for manipulation; on EB-Navigation (discrete move/rotate actions) GPT-4o scored 57.7%. That supports feeding LLM agents the same bounded-move interface, and undercuts any framing that MLLMs are generally poor at atomic actions.

X-Mobility as a sim baseline has an unflagged compatibility risk. The demo targets Isaac Sim 4.2 on Ubuntu 22.04 with ROS 2 Humble, and TensorRT engines must be rebuilt for the target GPU. The student has Isaac Sim 5.1 built from source on aarch64. No source confirms X-Mobility works on that stack, and it needs a route from robot position, so it depends entirely on the classical localizer.

The spark-projects pi0.5 figure (~94.7 ms) claims to 'match the Jetson Thor reference (~94 ms)', but NVIDIA's official Thor page reports ~49 ms (FP8+NVFP4) and ~132 ms BF16. Treat the community number as unverified, not as proof of parity.

research.summary: Yes, a credible benchmark is possible, and every metric it needs already exists. For localisation and mapping there are ATE (align the trajectories with Horn/Umeyama, then take the RMSE) and RPE (drift over a fixed interval) from Sturm et al. 2012, both implemented in evo, which reads ROS 2 bags directly. Kümmerle et al. 2009 note that metrics built on landmark positions need known data association (which estimated landmark is which real one). AprilTag IDs supply that for free, so tag-position RMSE is a valid map metric here. For exploration and navigation, Anderson et al. 2018 (arXiv:1807.06757) define success and SPL: a DONE action, a success radius of 2× body width, geodesic path lengths, and an explicit statement of which sensors the agent gets. Coverage (Chaplot 2020) and the times to reach 90% and 99% exploration (Xu 2022, Explore-Bench) measure exploration efficiency. Existing LLM/VLM embodied benchmarks, for example EmbodiedBench (temperature 0, one run, 20-step cap), mostly report one-shot success rates with no statistical testing. Spatial-reasoning benchmarks consistently find that LLMs break down on long-horizon sequential spatial tracking (PPNL, Lost in Aggregation, CubeBench). Structured memories or explicit cognitive maps help (Thinking on Maps, VSI-Bench). Simulation tooling is available: a Gazebo Harmonic AprilTag model generator; OdometryPublisher for ground-truth pose (DiffDrive odometry for realistic, error-prone odometry); ros_gz_bridge and ros_gz_sim create; and in Isaac Sim 5.1, an AprilTag MDL material, a ground-truth transform publisher and Replicator randomisation (5.1 is flagged as unsupported). For fair comparisons with few episodes, the sources agree on paired designs (Miller 2024) and bootstrap confidence intervals (with the caveat that they are too narrow at about 3 runs). They also recommend exact McNemar for binary outcomes, Wilcoxon for two systems and Friedman for many (Demšar 2006), and Holm correction. Real-robot trials should be interleaved and blind (Kress-Gazit 2024), sequential stopping rules (STEP) can cut the number of trials, and sim–real agreement can be checked with MMRV plus Pearson (SIMPLER). LLM outputs vary between runs even at temperature 0 (Atil 2024; Thinking Machines), so each world seed needs repeated runs.

claims.claim: ATE (Sturm et al., 'A Benchmark for the Evaluation of RGB-D SLAM Systems', Jürgen Sturm, IROS 2012) first rigidly aligns the estimated trajectory to ground truth with Horn's closed-form method, then takes the RMSE of the translational errors.
claims.quote: This can be achieved in closed form using the method of Horn [46], which finds the rigid-body transformation S corresponding to the least-squares solution that maps the estimated trajectory P1:n onto the ground truth trajectory Q1:n.

claims.claim: RPE measures local drift over a fixed interval Δ. The same paper warns against Δ = n (start compared with end) and recommends averaging over all Δ when evaluating SLAM.
claims.quote: The relative pose error measures the local accuracy of the trajectory over a fixed time interval ∆. Therefore, the relative pose error corresponds to the drift of the trajectory ... a common (but poor) choice is to set ∆ = n

claims.claim: evo computes APE and RPE and reads TUM, KITTI and EuRoC files plus ROS 1/ROS 2 bags, with no ROS installation needed.
claims.quote: This allows you also to read ROS 1 & 2 bags even if you don't have one of those ROS distros installed.

claims.claim: evo supports Umeyama alignment in SE(3) or Sim(3) (with scale), and RPE deltas can be expressed in metres.
claims.quote: `--align --correct_scale` or `-as` = Sim(3) Umeyama alignment (rotation, translation, scale)

claims.claim: In feature-based SLAM, maps are commonly scored by the distance between estimated and true landmark positions. Such metrics require known data association between estimated and true landmarks.
claims.quote: Note that all metrics measuring an error based on landmark locations require such a data association as given.

claims.claim: Filter consistency is measured with NEES averaged over many Monte Carlo runs. A single run's NEES is not an adequate test (Bailey et al., 'Consistency of the EKF-SLAM Algorithm', IROS 2006).
claims.quote: single run NEES is an inadequate measure of filter consistency, as the error sequence is correlated and does not follow a χ2 distribution.

claims.claim: SPL definition (Anderson et al., 'On Evaluation of Embodied Navigation Agents', Peter Anderson, 2018, arXiv:1807.06757): success is judged when the agent issues DONE, within a threshold defaulting to 2× body width, using geodesic distance.
claims.quote: We will refer to this measure as SPL, short for Success weighted by (normalized inverse) Path Length.

claims.claim: Anderson et al. recommend a DONE action evaluated at the moment it is issued, a default 2× body-width threshold, and an explicit statement of the agent's sensors (e.g., perfect odometry).
claims.quote: if the method assumes perfect odometry or GPS for localization, this must be stated explicitly.

claims.claim: Anderson et al. describe SPL as stringent: on unseen environments they would already count SPL of about 0.5 as good.
claims.quote: When evaluation is conducted in reasonably complex environments that have not been seen before, we expect an SPL of 0.5 to be a good level of navigation performance.

claims.claim: Exploration coverage (Chaplot et al., 'Learning to Explore using Active Neural SLAM', Devendra Singh Chaplot, 2020, arXiv:2004.05155) is known-traversable area, reported in m² and as a percentage, under a fixed step budget.
claims.quote: Coverage is the total area in the map known to be traversable.

claims.claim: Explore-Bench (Yuanfan Xu, 2022, arXiv:2202.11931) proposes two time-based efficiency metrics: time to 99% and time to 90% exploration.
claims.quote: The total time Ttotal when the exploration ratio is 99%. • The time Ttopo when the exploration ratio is 90%.

claims.claim: EmbodiedBench (Rui Yang, 2025, arXiv:2502.09560) has 1,128 tasks and evaluated 24 MLLMs. Its EB-Navigation track (AI2-THOR, 300 cases, max 20 steps) runs every model at temperature 0, and the paper reports no repeated runs or significance tests.
claims.quote: All models were "set with a temperature of 0 and a maximum completion token length of 2048."

claims.claim: EmbodiedBench reports that removing visual input sharply degrades navigation.
claims.quote: GPT-4o's EB-Navigation performance to drop sharply from 57.7% to 17.4%, with long-horizon planning completely collapsing to 0%

claims.claim: PPNL ('Can Large Language Models be Good Path Planners? A Benchmark and Investigation on Spatial-temporal Reasoning', Mohamed Aghzal, 2023, arXiv:2310.03249) finds GPT-4 does better when reasoning and acting are interleaved but still fails at long-term temporal reasoning.
claims.quote: still fails to perform long-term temporal reasoning

claims.claim: 'Lost in Aggregation' (Yuhan Jiang, 2026, arXiv:2606.22219): structured coordinate text beats rendered images, and one-shot maze navigation collapses to near zero by 10x10 for every model tested.
claims.quote: structured coordinate text is the most navigable, far surpassing rendered images

claims.claim: 'Thinking on Maps' (Zhiwei Wei, 2025, arXiv:2512.24504) finds structured (sequential or graph) memory drives spatial-task performance, and that performance saturates with scale.
claims.quote: structured memories particularly sequential and graph-based representations, substantially improving performance on structure-intensive tasks such as path planning

claims.claim: CubeBench (Huan-ang Gao, 2025, arXiv:2512.23328) tests spatial reasoning, long-horizon state tracking and active exploration under partial observation. Every tested LLM scored 0% on the long-horizon tasks.
claims.quote: a uniform 0.00% pass rate on all long-horizon tasks

claims.claim: VSI-Bench ('Thinking in Space', Jihan Yang, 2024, arXiv:2412.14171): explicitly generating a cognitive map improves MLLM distance reasoning, while CoT, self-consistency and tree-of-thoughts do not help.
claims.quote: explicitly generating cognitive maps during question-answering enhances MLLMs' spatial distance ability

claims.claim: VLABench (Shiduo Zhang, 2024, arXiv:2412.18194) evaluates both pretrained VLAs and VLM-based workflows, and finds both struggle.
claims.quote: both the current state-of-the-art pretrained VLAs and the workflow based on VLMs face challenges in our tasks

claims.claim: Embodied Agent Interface (Manling Li, 2024, arXiv:2410.07166) argues for breaking evaluation into error types (e.g., hallucination, affordance, planning) rather than reporting only the final success rate.
claims.quote: existing evaluations tend to rely solely on a final success rate, making it difficult to pinpoint what ability is missing.

claims.claim: VLMnav (Dylan Goetting, 2024, arXiv:2411.05755) uses a VLM as a zero-shot end-to-end navigation policy and reports SR and SPL on the HM3D ObjectNav and GOAT-Bench 'val unseen' splits, using a single VLM (Gemini Flash).
claims.quote: We use Gemini Flash as the VLM for all our experiments, given its low cost and high effectiveness.

claims.claim: A Gazebo Harmonic fork of gazebo_apriltag generates AprilTag models. The original (Gazebo Classic) repo ships tag36h11 models and a generate.py script.
claims.quote: Generates AprilTag models compatible with Gazebo Harmonic.

claims.claim: The officially supported ROS 2 pairing for Gazebo Harmonic is Jazzy; Humble works 'with caution'.
claims.quote: ROS 2 Jazzy (LTS) is the recommended combination with Gazebo Harmonic

claims.claim: ros_gz_bridge maps Gazebo and ROS 2 topics using a /TOPIC@ROS_MSG@GZ_MSG syntax or a YAML file.
claims.quote: /TOPIC@ROS_MSG@GZ_MSG

claims.claim: gz-sim's OdometryPublisher can attach to any entity to publish 2D/3D odometry; its Gaussian noise defaults to 0, so it serves as ground truth. A maintainer-facing issue notes that DiffDrive odometry, by contrast, contains physical errors.
claims.quote: odometry publisher has ground truth information while diff drive can include physical errors such as wrong wheel radius, wheel separation or possible wheel slips.

claims.claim: OdometryPublisher's parameters include gaussian_noise, which defaults to 0.
claims.quote: Standard deviation of the Gaussian noise to be added to pose and twist messages. This element is optional, and the default value is 0.

claims.claim: Models can be spawned into a running Harmonic world from ROS 2 at given x, y, z, which makes scripted, seeded placement of tags and obstacles possible.

claims.claim: SDF2MAP converts Gazebo SDF worlds into ROS occupancy grids (.pgm/.yaml). Those grids can serve as the denominator for coverage and as the basis for geodesic distances.
claims.quote: SDF2MAP is a lightweight desktop tool that converts Gazebo SDF / World files into 2D occupancy grid maps compatible with the ROS navigation stack.

claims.quote: Transforms your ideas into fully-functional Gazebo Classic simulations

claims.claim: ProcTHOR (Matt Deitke, 2022, arXiv:2206.06994) is the canonical example of procedural generation for evaluating embodied agents on unseen environments.
claims.quote: ProcTHOR enables us to sample arbitrarily large datasets of diverse, interactive, customizable, and performant virtual environments

claims.claim: Isaac Sim 5.1 ships an AprilTag MDL material that indexes into a tag mosaic image such as tag36h11.png. Its parameters are Mosaic texture, Tag Size, Tags Per Row, Spacing and Tag ID.
claims.quote: Mosaic texture ... Tag Size ... Tags Per Row ... Spacing ... Tag ID

claims.quote: add in another _ROS2 Publish Raw Transform Tree_ node to the graph

claims.claim: Isaac Sim 5.1's Replicator AMR-navigation tutorial (Nova Carter) randomises asset poses and swaps background environments from a standalone Python app.
claims.quote: Randomize poses of assets in the scene

claims.claim: The Isaac Sim 5.1 release notes list DGX Spark support and say live-streaming is not supported on aarch64. The ROS 2 CameraInfo message always has fy == fx.
claims.quote: Live-streaming is not yet supported on aarch64.
