claims.quote: Unsupported release: Isaac Sim 5.1.0 is no longer supported. Bug fixes and new features are delivered only in newer releases.

claims.claim: Miller ('Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations', Evan Miller, 2024, arXiv:2411.00640) makes five recommendations: CLT standard errors; clustered SEs when items are grouped; resampling answers to cut variance; paired per-question differences; and power analysis.
claims.quote: When two models are being compared, conducting statistical inference on the questionlevel paired differences, rather than the population-level summary statistics

claims.claim: Miller shows that pairing lowers variance for free when item scores are positively correlated, and that clustered SEs can be far larger than naive ones.
claims.quote: paired differences represent a “free” reduction in estimator variance when comparing two models

claims.claim: Agarwal et al. ('Deep Reinforcement Learning at the Edge of the Statistical Precipice', Rishabh Agarwal, 2021, arXiv:2108.13264) recommend stratified bootstrap CIs and IQM when runs are few, but warn that bootstrap CIs undercover at 3 runs.
claims.quote: with 3 runs, bootstrap CIs underestimate the true 95% CIs and might require a larger nominal coverage rate to achieve true 95% coverage.

claims.claim: Kress-Gazit et al. ('Robot Learning as an Empirical Science: Best Practices for Policy Evaluation', Hadas Kress-Gazit, 2024, arXiv:2409.09491) recommend: report initial conditions and success criteria; match initial conditions; interleave policies blind to the evaluator within one session; run statistical analysis (frequentist or Bayesian).
claims.quote: A/B testing, i.e., interleaving policy rollouts when comparing different policies in a way that is blind to the evaluator.

claims.claim: Kress-Gazit et al. note that simulation makes identical initial conditions and automated metrics easy, at the cost of having to reason about the sim-to-real gap.
claims.quote: ensuring identical initial condition and environmental state (lighting, friction, etc) and automating all the metrics, at the expense of needing to reason about the sim-to-real gap.

claims.claim: Dietterich (1998, Neural Computation 10(7)) finds McNemar's test is the only acceptable test when each algorithm can be run only once.
claims.quote: For algorithms that can be executed only once, Mc-Nemar's test is the only test with acceptable type I error.

claims.claim: Raschka (arXiv:1811.12808) says to use the exact binomial McNemar when discordant counts are small. For three or more models it gives Cochran's Q as the omnibus test, followed by pairwise McNemar with a correction.
claims.quote: it makes sense to use a computationally more expensive binomial test to compute the exact p-values if the values of B and C are relatively small

claims.claim: Demšar (JMLR 2006, 'Statistical Comparisons of Classifiers over Multiple Data Sets') recommends the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for two methods and Friedman with post-hoc tests for more.
claims.quote: the Wilcoxon signed ranks test for comparison of two classifiers and the Friedman test with the corresponding post-hoc tests for comparison of more classifiers over multiple data sets.

claims.claim: Holm's step-down procedure (1979) controls the familywise error rate and is available in statsmodels.
claims.quote: holm: step-down method using Bonferroni adjustments

claims.claim: SciPy's wilcoxon handles paired samples and uses the exact distribution by default for small n (≤50). scipy.stats.bootstrap supports paired resampling.
claims.quote: When `len(d)` is small, the normal approximation may not be accurate, and `method='exact'` is preferred.

claims.claim: The SciPy bootstrap 'paired' option resamples the same indices across all arrays.
claims.quote: If True, bootstrap resamples an array of indices and uses the same indices for all arrays in data

claims.claim: STEP ('Is Your Imitation Learning Policy Better than Mine? Policy Comparison with Near-Optimal Stopping', David Snyder, 2025, arXiv:2503.10966) is a sequential test for small real-robot budgets (about 10–50 trials) that preserves error control.
claims.quote: reduces the number of evaluation trials by up to 32% as compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while preserving the probabilistic correctness and statistical power

claims.claim: Snyder et al. 2026 (arXiv:2603.13616) extends safe anytime-valid sequential comparison to continuous and partial-credit metrics. Policies separate faster on fine-grained progress metrics than on binary success.
claims.quote: competing policies can be separated more quickly when using fine-grained task progress than binary success metrics

claims.claim: SIMPLER (Xuanlin Li, 2024, arXiv:2405.05941) shows through paired sim-and-real evaluations that sim correlates with real. It proposes MMRV, a margin-weighted rank-violation metric, because Pearson r alone is unreliable.
claims.quote: Pearson correlation does not reflect the range of values it is computed over.

claims.claim: The 2026 VLA sim-real study (Shuo Wang, arXiv:2606.10366) judges a simulator by ranking consistency, performance correlation and failure patterns under perturbations.
claims.quote: measuring whether simulated evaluation preserves real-world conclusions in terms of policy ranking consistency, performance correlation, and perturbation-wise failure patterns.

claims.claim: Settings meant to be deterministic are not: temperature-0 LLM runs vary noticeably (Berk Atil, 'Non-Determinism of "Deterministic" LLM Settings', 2024, arXiv:2408.04667).
claims.quote: We see accuracy variations up to 15% across naturally occurring runs with a gap of best possible performance to worst possible performance up to 70%.

claims.claim: Thinking Machines attributes endpoint nondeterminism mainly to batch-size variation. Its batch-invariant kernels made 1000 temperature-0 vLLM completions identical, at a speed cost.
claims.quote: the primary reason nearly all LLM inference endpoints are nondeterministic is that the load (and thus batch-size) nondeterministically varies.

claims.claim: 'AI Agents That Matter' (Sayash Kapoor, 2024, arXiv:2407.01502) argues for optimising accuracy and cost jointly, and warns that agent benchmarks often lack holdout sets.
claims.quote: many agent benchmarks have inadequate holdout sets, and sometimes none at all

claims.claim: A cheap overhead camera tracking an AprilTag on the robot's top plate gave about 0.8 cm average error on a 2.5 × 1.75 m testbed and served as ground truth (HeRoSwarm, Michael Starks, 2022, arXiv:2211.03014).
claims.quote: the average error of the camera-based positioning system is 0.8 cm, meaning a reasonable sub-cm accuracy for using it as ground truth in robot tracking and performance evaluations.

claims.claim: GroundGazer (Sven Hinderer, 2025, arXiv:2509.17346) is a low-cost planar reference system (monocular fisheye camera plus chessboard floor) with mm-level position and sub-degree heading accuracy.
claims.quote: GG estimates the AMR's planar position with mm and its heading with sub-degree accuracy.

claims.claim: TagSLAM (Bernd Pfrommer, 2019, arXiv:1910.00679) is an open-source ROS front end to GTSAM for AprilTag SLAM, loop closure and ground-truth localisation, so it could serve as a classical baseline.
claims.quote: full SLAM, extrinsic camera calibration with non-overlapping views, visual localization for ground truth, loop closure for odometry, pose estimation etc.

claims.claim: Loop-closure and place-recognition detection is scored with precision/recall, AUPRC and R@100P. With robust back-ends, finding enough true loop closures matters more than avoiding every false one (Schubert et al., 'Visual Place Recognition: A Tutorial', 2023, arXiv:2303.03281).
claims.quote: With robust graph optimization, it is more important to find enough correct loop closures (T P ) than to avoid wrong loop closures (F P ).

claims.claim: Arena 4.0 (Volodymyr Shcherbyna, 2024, arXiv:2409.12471) generates ROS 2 navigation benchmark worlds with LLMs and diffusion models from text prompts or floorplans.
claims.quote: large language models (LLMs) and diffusion models to dynamically generate complex, human-centric environments from text prompts or 2D floorplans

implications: INFERENCE (metric suite): score each episode on four layers. (A) Localisation and map: ATE-RMSE after SE(2) Umeyama alignment of the pose belief the LLM commits at each decision step, computed with evo from a ROS 2 bag; RPE per 1 m; tag-map RMSE after the same alignment (valid because tag IDs give data association for free); tag-ID precision/recall to catch hallucinated or missed tags; loop-closure precision/recall against ground-truth revisits. (B) Exploration: share of tags found and share of area covered as functions of distance, steps and wall-clock time, plus time to 90% and 99% of tags found. (C) Post-mapping navigation ('go to tag k', 'return home') using the agent's own map: success and SPL with a DONE action, a 2× body-width threshold and geodesics from the ground-truth occupancy grid. (D) Cost: tokens, $ per episode, latency per decision, and the rate of invalid tool calls.

INFERENCE (the key to credibility): run two evaluation modes. (1) Open-loop replay: record sensor logs once, in sim and on the real robot (odometry, AprilTag detections as ID+range+bearing, JPEG frames), and feed the identical sequence to every model. Every model then sees the same observations, so ATE and map error differ only by reasoning, and replay is cheap to repeat. (2) Closed-loop: the model also chooses where to go, which tests exploration. Without mode 1, a model that explored badly also sees fewer tags, and its ATE is confounded.

INFERENCE (baselines): include wheel-odometry dead-reckoning as the floor; a classical EKF-SLAM or GTSAM/TagSLAM estimator on the same tag detections as the reference ceiling; random and frontier exploration; and an oracle-pose condition that isolates exploration and decision quality from localisation. Without a classical baseline, 'LLM as SLAM' results cannot be interpreted.

INFERENCE (isolate reasoning from perception): give all text-LLM conditions the same AprilTag detector outputs. Add a VLM image-only condition, where the model must detect and read tags itself, as a separate ablation. State inputs explicitly (odometry given or not, IMU heading given or not), as Anderson et al. require. Given the Thinking on Maps and VSI-Bench results, also compare 'structured map-memory tool' against 'raw history in context', because the memory scaffold may matter more than the model.

INFERENCE (VLA/navigation foundation models): end-to-end VLA or navigation-diffusion policies (e.g. NoMaD) do not output a pose or a landmark map. Score them only on layers B and C as exploration baselines, not in the ATE or map tables.

INFERENCE (sim tooling for this project): use Gazebo Harmonic with ROS 2 Jazzy (the officially paired distro) as the main generator of many seeded worlds. A small Python generator can write seeded SDF arenas (walls and boxes, N tag36h11 models from the Harmonic gazebo_apriltag fork at random wall poses) or spawn them with ros_gz_sim create. OdometryPublisher (noise 0) provides ground truth and DiffDrive provides realistic, error-prone odometry, all bridged with ros_gz_bridge. SDF2MAP produces the occupancy grid used for coverage and geodesics. Separate dev seeds (for prompt tuning) from held-out test seeds (Kapoor et al.). Use Isaac Sim 5.1 (AprilTag.mdl, Raw Transform Tree for ground truth, Replicator randomisation) only for a small photoreal subset: 5.1 is flagged unsupported, live-streaming does not work on aarch64, and the Gazebo pipeline alone already yields a valid benchmark.

INFERENCE (ESP32-CAM realism): in sim, degrade camera frames to match the OV3660 over Wi-Fi (low resolution, JPEG artefacts, latency, dropped frames). Measure the real detector's tag range, bearing noise and detection range once, and inject the same noise into the simulated detections, so the sim-to-real step does not change the estimator's inputs.

INFERENCE (episode counts; my arithmetic with scipy exact tests): with n paired episodes, the smallest two-sided p-value an exact Wilcoxon or sign/McNemar test can reach is 2/2^n. So n=5 gives at best 0.0625, n=6 gives 0.031, n=9 gives 0.0039 and n=10 gives 0.0020. Comparing 6 models pairwise means 15 tests, so Holm's first threshold is 0.05/15 ≈ 0.0033, which needs at least 10 paired episodes even if one model wins every episode. Real-world trials should therefore test only 2–3 pre-registered comparisons (e.g. best frontier model vs best local model vs classical baseline) with at least 10 paired episodes each, or use STEP/SAVI sequential stopping. The full many-model comparison belongs in sim, e.g. about 30–50 held-out seeds × K≥3 repeats.

INFERENCE (analysis plan to pre-register): name one primary endpoint per mode (e.g. ATE-RMSE in replay, tags found within a fixed budget in closed loop). Run Friedman across all models, then pairwise Wilcoxon on per-seed means with Holm correction. Report paired, world-clustered bootstrap percentile CIs of the differences. Test binary success with exact McNemar, or Cochran's Q for many models. Report IQM next to the mean because failures cause heavy tails, and show cost-versus-accuracy Pareto plots. Use a pilot to estimate variance and run Miller-style power analysis before fixing n.

INFERENCE (nondeterminism): because temperature 0 is not deterministic, run K≥3 repeats per seed and average them before the paired tests. For local vLLM models, either enable batch-invariant or deterministic mode or send requests one at a time. Log exact model IDs or dates, the system-prompt hash and the tool schema version, because frontier API models change silently.

INFERENCE (real-world protocol): build 2–4 arena layouts with tape-measured tag poses, and give each layout a matched Gazebo digital twin. Obtain ground truth from an overhead camera tracking a large AprilTag on top of the robot, using a tag ID range the robot never uses as a beacon; the HeRoSwarm result suggests about 1 cm on a table-sized field (unverified for larger arenas). Fix the start poses, interleave models in a Latin-square order within one session with a blind operator, and log battery voltage, since 4×AA sag affects motion. Then report sim–real agreement per model with MMRV and Pearson. Only if the rankings agree (low MMRV) can the large sim comparison be said to predict real performance.

INFERENCE (effect on D1 feasibility and risk): published spatial-reasoning benchmarks (PPNL, Lost in Aggregation, CubeBench) show LLMs failing at long-horizon sequential spatial tracking. Expect raw-context LLM localisation to drift far worse than an EKF over long runs. The benchmark stays scientifically meaningful, but the headline finding may be 'which scaffolding lets an LLM approach a classical estimator', not 'LLMs do SLAM'. Frame the hypotheses that way before collecting data.
unknowns: No published benchmark was found that scores LLMs/VLMs as SLAM estimators (pose and landmark map) with ATE or map RMSE. The closest work is text or grid spatial benchmarks (PPNL, CubeBench, Thinking on Maps) and VLM navigation (VLMnav, EmbodiedBench), so the protocol above is new and cannot be checked against prior results.

No maintained procedural world generator for Gazebo Harmonic (gz-sim) was found. The ones found target Gazebo Classic (nav2_random_map_generator, robotics-upo gazebo_world_generator), and SDF2MAP's supported Gazebo version is not stated. A custom seeded SDF generator is probably needed.

verdicts.claim: ATE (Sturm et al. IROS 2012) aligns with Horn's closed-form method, then takes RMSE of translational errors.
verdicts.note: The PDF text has 'of Horn [46], which finds the rigid-body transformation S' and defines ATE as the RMSE of the translational components.

verdicts.claim: RPE measures drift over a fixed interval Δ; the paper warns against Δ = n and recommends averaging over all Δ for SLAM.
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'a common (but poor) choice is to set ∆ = n ... For the evaluation of SLAM systems, it therefore makes sense to average over all possible time intervals ∆'.

verdicts.claim: evo computes APE/RPE and reads TUM, KITTI, EuRoC and ROS 1/ROS 2 bags without a ROS install.
verdicts.note: The substance holds, but the README I fetched is worded differently from the researcher's quote: 'Reading ROS bag files works also without a ROS installation thanks to the great rosbags package'. It lists TUM, KITTI, EuRoC and 'ROS and ROS2 bagfile'.

verdicts.claim: evo supports SE(3)/Sim(3) Umeyama alignment, and RPE deltas can be in metres.
verdicts.note: The wiki lists '-a' as SE(3), '-as' as Sim(3) and '--delta_unit m'. It also has '--project_to_plane {xy,xz,yz}'. There is no native SE(2) alignment option (relevant to Implication 1).

verdicts.claim: In feature-based SLAM, maps are commonly scored by landmark distance, and such metrics require known data association (Kümmerle 2009).
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim (Autonomous Robots paper 'On Measuring the Accuracy of SLAM Algorithms', Rainer Kümmerle). The passage does not say landmark scoring is 'common', though. Kümmerle presents it as option (b) and then says 'we would recommend the first option [trajectory recovered by localization in the built map] to evaluate techniques such as EKF'. Their metric is also a relative-displacement metric, not an aligned absolute RMSE.

verdicts.claim: NEES must be averaged over Monte Carlo runs; single-run NEES is inadequate (Bailey et al. IROS 2006).
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'single run NEES is an inadequate measure of filter consistency, as the error sequence is correlated'. Only relevant if the LLM emits a covariance, which the researcher did not address.

verdicts.claim: SPL definition (Anderson et al. 2018, arXiv:1807.06757): DONE action, 2× body-width threshold, geodesic distance.
verdicts.note: PDF text: 'we consider the configuration of the agent at the time it outputs the action DONE', 'threshold of 2× the agent's body width is used by default', 'we recommend using the geodesic'.

verdicts.claim: Anderson et al. require explicitly stating sensors such as perfect odometry.
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'if the method assumes perfect odometry or GPS for localization, this must be stated explicitly.'

verdicts.claim: Anderson et al.: an SPL of about 0.5 is good in unseen environments.
verdicts.note: The text has 'have not been seen before, we expect an SPL of 0.5 to be' a good level.

verdicts.claim: Coverage (Chaplot et al. 2020, arXiv:2004.05155) is known-traversable area, in m² and %, under a fixed step budget.
verdicts.note: 'Coverage is the total area in the map known to be traversable... absolute coverage area in m2 (Cov) and the percentage of area explored'. The evaluation is in Habitat simulation.

verdicts.claim: Explore-Bench (Xu 2022, arXiv:2202.11931) uses time to 99% (Ttotal) and time to 90% (Ttopo) exploration.
verdicts.note: The quote appears verbatim. These are area-exploration ratios. Using them as '90%/99% of tags found' (Implication 1) is an adaptation, not the paper's metric.

verdicts.claim: EmbodiedBench (Yang 2025, arXiv:2502.09560): 1,128 tasks, 24 MLLMs; EB-Navigation has 300 cases and max 20 steps; temperature 0; no repeated runs or significance tests.
verdicts.note: The cited v1 HTML says '13 leading proprietary and open-source MLLMs'. Only the current abstract says 24, so the claim mixes versions. Confirmed: 300 cases, max 20 steps, temperature 0. 'No repeated runs or significance tests' was checked only against v1 main results; later versions were not verified. EB-Navigation runs in AI2-THOR simulation.

verdicts.claim: PPNL (Aghzal 2023, arXiv:2310.03249): GPT-4 improves when reasoning and acting are interleaved but still fails long-term temporal reasoning.
verdicts.note: Abstract: 'prompted to reason and act interleavedly, although it still fails to perform long-term temporal reasoning'. The setting is synthetic grid path planning, not a robot.

verdicts.claim: CubeBench (Gao 2025, arXiv:2512.23328): every tested LLM scored 0% on long-horizon tasks.

verdicts.note: The text has 'with 3 runs, bootstrap CIs underestimate the true 95% CIs and might require a larger nominal coverage rate'. The context is RL benchmarks.

verdicts.claim: Kress-Gazit: simulation gives identical initial conditions at the cost of the sim-to-real gap.
verdicts.note: Verbatim at line ~438 of the extracted text.

verdicts.claim: Dietterich 1998: McNemar is the only acceptable test when algorithms run once.
verdicts.note: Verbatim. The context is supervised classifiers and only the five tests studied, so applying it to LLM episodes is an analogy.

verdicts.claim: Raschka: exact binomial McNemar for small discordant counts; Cochran's Q omnibus then pairwise McNemar with correction.
verdicts.note: The binomial quote is verbatim. Cochran's Q is described as 'a generalized version of McNemar's test for three or more models', followed by 'McNemar's test with a Bonferroni correction'. Raschka's example uses Bonferroni, not Holm.

verdicts.claim: Demšar 2006: Wilcoxon for two, Friedman with post-hoc for more.
verdicts.note: Verbatim. Note that Benavoli et al. 2016 later argued against Demšar's mean-ranks post-hoc tests (see Missed).

verdicts.claim: Holm is available in statsmodels.
verdicts.note: 'holm : step-down method using Bonferroni adjustments'. The default method is 'hs', not 'holm', so method='holm' must be passed explicitly.

verdicts.claim: SciPy wilcoxon uses the exact distribution by default for n ≤ 50.
verdicts.note: SciPy 1.18 docs: exact is used when len(d) <= 50 only without ties or zeros. With ties or zeros, exhaustive permutations are used when len(d) <= 13, and the asymptotic method otherwise. The default zero_method='wilcox' discards zero differences, which shrinks the effective n.

verdicts.claim: The scipy.stats.bootstrap paired option resamples the same indices.
verdicts.note: Verbatim. The default method is BCa, which can return NaN on degenerate data (e.g. all-success samples).

verdicts.claim: STEP (Snyder 2025, arXiv:2503.10966): a sequential test for about 10–50 trials with error control; up to 32% fewer trials.
verdicts.note: The abstract says '(e.g., 10 or 50)' and 'up to 32%'. It compares two policies with binary success in imitation-learning manipulation, so it is not multi-model and not navigation.

verdicts.claim: Snyder 2026 (arXiv:2603.13616) extends anytime-valid comparison to continuous and partial metrics; fine-grained progress separates policies faster.
verdicts.note: Title: 'Beyond Binary Success: Sample-Efficient and Statistically Rigorous Robot Policy Comparison', submitted 13 Mar 2026. The domain is manipulation.

verdicts.claim: SIMPLER (Li 2024): sim correlates with real; MMRV proposed because Pearson alone is unreliable.
verdicts.note: 'Pearson correlation does not reflect the range of values it is computed over... we propose the Mean Maximum Rank Violation (MMRV)'. Both metrics are reported. The domain is manipulation policies.

verdicts.note: Title: 'A Practical Recipe Towards Improving Sim-and-Real Correlation for VLA Evaluation', 9 Jun 2026. It covers VLA policies (manipulation), not navigation.

verdicts.claim: Atil (arXiv:2408.04667): temperature-0 runs vary up to 15% accuracy, with a best-to-worst gap up to 70%.
verdicts.note: Current title 'Non-Determinism of "Deterministic" LLM Settings'. Five LLMs, 8 tasks, 10 runs, v5 dated Apr 2025.

verdicts.claim: Thinking Machines: batch-size variation causes nondeterminism; batch-invariant kernels give 1000 identical temperature-0 completions at a speed cost.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim. Qwen3-235B produced 80 unique completions without the kernels and 1 with them. The speed test (Qwen-3-8B on vLLM) took 26 s by default versus 42–55 s deterministic, roughly a 2× cost.

verdicts.claim: Kapoor 2024: optimise cost and accuracy jointly; agent benchmarks often lack holdouts.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim.

verdicts.claim: HeRoSwarm (Starks 2022): an overhead camera tracking an AprilTag on the robot's top plate gave about 0.8 cm error on a 2.5×1.75 m testbed, used as ground truth.
verdicts.note: The 0.8 cm figure comes from static AprilTags placed on marked points on the board, not from a moving robot. Error in dynamic tracking (motion blur, latency, tag height above the floor) was not characterised.

verdicts.claim: GroundGazer (Hinderer 2025): mm position and sub-degree heading from a fisheye camera and chessboard floor.
verdicts.note: Verbatim. v5 is dated Mar 2026. It needs a chessboard floor, which constrains the arena.

verdicts.claim: TagSLAM (Pfrommer 2019): ROS front end to GTSAM for AprilTag SLAM, loop closure and ground truth.
verdicts.note: The abstract matches. Its maintenance and ROS 2 status were not verified in this check.

verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim. It is explicitly conditional on 'robust graph optimization'.

verdicts.note: Verbatim. The paper also migrates to Gazebo Garden (new gz-sim), which contradicts the researcher's 'Classic-only' conclusion.

implication_challenges: The Isaac Sim tooling implication (and the verdict above) relies on a misread release note. The 5.1 notes FIXED CameraInfo so that it no longer always sets fy = fx. Also, 5.1 has been superseded by Isaac Sim 6.0 (general availability announced 8 Jun 2026). The recommendation should say: evaluate 6.0 on aarch64 before committing to the unsupported 5.1 build. The 'which release supersedes 5.1' unknown is answerable.

Implication 1 ('ATE after SE(2) Umeyama alignment with evo'): evo offers SE(3) or Sim(3) Umeyama plus --project_to_plane xy, not a native SE(2) alignment. For planar data this is workable, but it should be stated as project-to-plane followed by SE(3) alignment, or implemented as a custom SE(2) Umeyama. Also, aligning the LLM's pose belief frees the evaluation from the arbitrary map frame. That suits SLAM, but it hides a systematic heading bias that a single rigid transform can absorb. RPE and tag-map error must accompany ATE.

The loop-closure metric leans on Schubert et al. Their claim that true positives matter more than false positives is explicitly conditional on a robust graph back end. In an LLM-as-SLAM system there is no robust optimiser: one hallucinated revisit can corrupt the whole map. Loop-closure precision should therefore be weighted at least as heavily as recall, the opposite of what that citation suggests.

The tag-map RMSE 'valid because tag IDs give data association for free' holds only if the detector reads IDs correctly. With the ESP32-CAM at low resolution, ID misreads or the VLM hallucinating IDs break that assumption. Kümmerle et al. actually recommend trajectory-based evaluation over landmark-based evaluation for EKF-type methods. Tag-ID precision and recall (which the researcher includes) must gate the map RMSE.

The statistics transferred from STEP, SAVI (Snyder 2026), SIMPLER/MMRV, Kress-Gazit and Shuo Wang 2026 were all developed for manipulation policies, mostly with binary success. Their applicability to navigation or SLAM with continuous ATE is inference. MMRV in particular needs several models evaluated in real episodes to be meaningful; with 2–3 real models it has very little resolving power.

Episode-count arithmetic: the 2/2^n floor is correct for exact Wilcoxon or sign tests with no zero differences. SciPy's default zero_method='wilcox' drops ties, though, and exact mode is used only without ties or zeros (n ≤ 13 otherwise uses permutation). For McNemar, the floor depends on the number of DISCORDANT pairs, not on n. Two models that both succeed (or both fail) on most episodes need far more than 10 real episodes. The '≥10 paired episodes' rule is therefore a lower bound, not a sufficient number.

The analysis plan ('Friedman, then pairwise Wilcoxon with Holm') is defensible, but Demšar's own recommendation is Friedman with mean-rank post-hoc tests (Nemenyi and similar). Pairwise Wilcoxon is justified by Benavoli et al. 2016, which the researcher did not cite. Note too that statsmodels multipletests defaults to 'hs', not 'holm'.

Overhead-camera ground truth '~1 cm' comes from HeRoSwarm's static calibration of tags placed on marked points, not from tracking a moving robot. For a moving TT-motor car seen through a webcam, motion blur, latency relative to the robot's timestamps, and the parallax of the tag's height must be measured. The error budget is unverified, not '~1 cm'.

'Isaac Sim Replicator randomisation' for benchmark worlds: the cited tutorial is a pipeline for synthetic perception images, not an evaluation harness, so reusing it for seeded navigation worlds is extra engineering. Likewise, 'OdometryPublisher = ground truth' rests on a user's issue suggestion, not maintainer documentation. The origin frame (start pose or world) must be checked before computing ATE.

The claim that no gz-sim procedural generator exists is overstated. Arena 4.0 and Arena-Rosnav moved from Gazebo Classic to Gazebo Garden (new gz-sim), and advertise dynamic maze and map generation with repositories active in Sep 2026. Harmonic compatibility is unverified, but 'a custom generator is probably needed' should be downgraded to 'evaluate Arena first'.

The D1 risk framing ('LLMs fail at long-horizon spatial tracking') generalises from benchmarks that are text grids, mazes and Rubik's Cubes (PPNL, Lost in Aggregation, CubeBench) or video QA (VSI-Bench). None of them is a robot with odometry and fiducial range and bearing. The prediction that raw-context LLM localisation will drift worse than an EKF is plausible, but it is an extrapolation, not a finding.
Citing EmbodiedBench as '24 MLLMs, one run, no statistics' mixes paper versions: v1 says 13 models. The 'no statistics' observation was checked only against v1.
missed: Benavoli, Corani, Mangili, 'Should We Really Use Post-Hoc Tests Based on Mean-Ranks?', JMLR 17 (2016), arXiv:1505.02288. They show that the outcome of the mean-ranks post-hoc test depends on which algorithms are in the pool, and recommend the sign test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test instead. This is the proper justification for the researcher's 'Friedman then pairwise Wilcoxon + Holm' plan. https://jmlr.org/papers/v17/benavoli16a.html

The Gazebo docs now list Gz Jetty (LTS) as a newer LTS that pairs with ROS 2 Lyrical (LTS) and Kilted. Harmonic remains recommended with Jazzy, and Harmonic with Lyrical is 'Possible, but use with caution'. https://gazebosim.org/docs/harmonic/ros_installation/

evo supports '--project_to_plane {xy, xz, yz}' to reduce trajectories to 2D before computing errors, and '--delta_unit m' for per-metre RPE. This is the practical route for planar-robot ATE. https://github.com/MichaelGrupp/evo/wiki/Metrics

Arena 4.0 (arXiv:2409.12471) migrated from 'Gazebo Classic' to 'Gazebo Garden' (new gz-sim) and Nav2. The Arena-Rosnav GitHub organisation advertises 'Dynamic Map Generation including dynamic mazes', with repositories updated as recently as Sep 21, 2026 (arena-isaac). It is a candidate procedural-world source for gz-sim. https://github.com/Arena-Rosnav

Sirui Xia et al., 'Can LLMs Learn to Map the World from Local Descriptions?', 2025, arXiv:2505.20874. LLMs, grounded in local relative descriptions, 'infer consistent global layouts' and learn road connectivity in a simulated urban environment. This is closer prior work on LLMs building global maps from local observations than the grid benchmarks cited. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20874

SciPy 1.18 wilcoxon: exact is used for len(d) <= 50 only without ties or zeros. With ties or zeros, exhaustive permutation is used for len(d) <= 13, and the default zero_method='wilcox' discards zero differences. This matters for paired LLM episodes with identical outcomes. https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.wilcoxon.html
statsmodels multipletests defaults to method 'hs', not 'holm'; Holm must be requested explicitly. https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests.html

Kümmerle et al. 2009 ('On Measuring the Accuracy of SLAM Algorithms') recommend recovering the trajectory by localising in the built map with the SLAM system's own data association, rather than landmark-location metrics: 'we would recommend the first option to evaluate techniques such as EKF.' http://ais.informatik.uni-freiburg.de/publications/papers/kuemmerle09auro.pdf

VLMnav's authors warn that their simulation results depend on an 'allow slide' collision setting that 'would likely lead to collisions with obstacles in the real world'. This is a concrete sim-to-real caveat for VLM navigation baselines. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.05755

Isaac Sim's Isaac Compute Odometry node 'calculates the position of the robot relative to its start location'. Ground truth needs a separate world→odom Raw Transform Tree. https://docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com/5.1.0/ros2_tutorials/tutorial_ros2_tf.html
